items.title: Home
items.text:
HomeGAP is a self-hosted alternative to Cloudflare Tunnels and WARP. Your homelab is the only origin, and nothing at home accepts inbound connections. Regional VPS nodes take each viewer's connection near the viewer and send it home through a WireGuard tunnel that the homelab dials out.

One orchestrator container on the homelab controls the system from Docker labels:

  • Regional nodes are Ubuntu VPS servers from any provider, in any location. Each node runs Pangolin with Gerbil and Traefik.
  • Bunny DNS sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. Health checks remove a node that fails.
  • The orchestrator reads the labels and creates the Pangolin resources on every node, the tunnels that connect the nodes to the homelab, and the DNS records. It also installs and maintains the nodes over SSH.

Caution

HomeGAP is early-stage software. Test it on a domain that nothing depends on, for example a spare domain or a subdomain delegated to Bunny DNS. Then move production traffic to it.

items.title: Home
items.text:
Publish homelab services worldwide through your own regional edge nodes. No inbound ports, no third-party tunnel.

Getting started · How it works · Label reference

items.title: Features
items.text:
• The origin stays hidden. The homelab has no open ports. Every tunnel starts at home.
  • End-to-end TLS by default. Nodes route by the TLS server name and never see plaintext. One label moves TLS termination to the nodes. See Traffic paths.
  • HTTP(S), raw TCP and UDP, and private services that only the Pangolin client can reach. See Services.
  • Geo routing with failover. Each viewer reaches the nearest healthy node. See DNS routing and health checks.
  • A VPN that keeps working when the homelab is down. In cluster mode, all nodes are one Pangolin with shared users and devices. The Pangolin apps connect through the nearest node, and sign-in continues to work while the homelab is offline. See Cluster mode.
  • Real client addresses and private-only services. The homelab sees each viewer's address, and a Traefik allowlist can admit only Pangolin clients. See Client addresses.
  • One label publishes a service. Docker labels are the source of truth. The orchestrator makes the rest match them.
  • Node lifecycle from a bare VPS. A dashboard wizard turns a fresh server into a node over SSH. Updates roll out one node at a time, with automatic rollback. See Add a node.
  • A built-in dashboard for health, pausing, re-provisioning, speed tests, diagnostics and node management. It also serves this documentation for its own version. See The dashboard.
  • Self-hosted maps of the nodes and the homelab, on the dashboard and on an optional public status page. No third-party map service. See Maps and locations.
  • The orchestrator is never in the traffic path. If it stops, the nodes continue to serve, the tunnels stay up and DNS continues to resolve. You can manage each part by hand: SSH, each node's Pangolin dashboard, or the Bunny console.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
Start with Getting started. For the model behind the system, read How HomeGAP works.

These pages are the documentation for HomeGAP version dev.

items.title: License
items.text: HomeGAP has the MIT license. Pangolin has its own license terms. Two HomeGAP features need Pangolin EE: cluster mode, and wildcard resources with TLS ended on the nodes (terminate). Pangolin EE is free for personal use and for organizations below its commercial revenue threshold. See Pangolin EE licenses.

items.title: Cluster mode
items.text: In cluster mode, all nodes run one Pangolin EE cluster. This page tells you what cluster mode gives you, what it needs and how to enable it.

items.title: What cluster mode is
items.text: With cluster: in the config, the Pangolin of each node is one instance of a single Pangolin EE cluster. The instances use a shared database with a member on the homelab and on every node. The members connect over a private WireGuard mesh, hg-mesh. The cluster has one org, one set of users and one license.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
• The Pangolin apps connect to pangolin.<domain>, and DNS sends them to the nearest healthy node. The apps continue to work while the homelab is down, and sign-in also works. See Clustered Pangolin and Connect the Pangolin apps.
  • The Access page on the dashboard manages users and devices. See Users and devices.
  • The Pangolin apps can send all traffic of a device through a node or through the homelab. See Exit nodes.
  • One EE license key covers all nodes. See Pangolin EE licenses.

items.title: The parts
items.text:
Read the pages in this order. Each part builds on the part before it.

  1. Cluster mesh: the private WireGuard network between the members.
  2. Cluster database: PostgreSQL, Valkey and the vote.
  3. Clustered Pangolin: the Pangolin instances on the shared database.
  4. Users and devices: the Access page.
  5. Connect the Pangolin apps: the devices of your users.
  6. Exit nodes: exits to the internet for the apps.

Caution

Choose the mode when you deploy. HomeGAP does not support the addition or removal of cluster: on a deployment that runs. A node that HomeGAP provisions in one mode keeps the stack of that mode until you remove the node and add it again.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Two or more nodes. The vote needs a majority. With the homelab and only one node, the loss of either one stops all writes.
  • A decision about the role of the homelab, before the first start. The homelab can hold a copy of the database (the default) or only vote. See The homelab as a vote only.
  • WireGuard in the kernel of the homelab host. It is part of Linux 5.6 and later.
  • The homegap-mesh and homegap-mesh-agent services from deploy/homelab-compose.yml. The agent needs cap_add: [NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW].
  • cap_add: [NET_ADMIN] on the orchestrator, for its route to the mesh.
  • The cluster containers of the homelab from the same file: homegap-etcd, homegap-db, homegap-valkey and homegap-sentinel. They share the network namespace of homegap-mesh.

items.title: Enable cluster mode
items.text:
To use all the defaults, add this line to the config:

cluster: {}
Key Default Rules cluster.mesh.subnet 10.77.0.0/24 Must not overlap 100.64.0.0/10, the tunnel ranges of Pangolin. Must have space for the maximum of 32 nodes. Use /26 or larger. cluster.mesh.port 51821 A UDP port. Must be different from 51820 and 21820. cluster.image ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap-cluster:latest Must not be empty. cluster.primary.preferred homelab homelab is the only accepted value. cluster.primary.switch_back_after 10m The time that the homelab must stay caught up before it becomes the primary again. cluster.client_hostname pangolin The first label of the client address, <client_hostname>.<domain>. cluster.exit_nodes.nodes false Offers an exit through each node. cluster.exit_nodes.homelab false Offers an exit through the homelab. cluster.exit_nodes.roles [] The roles that can use the exits. cluster.exit_nodes.newt_image docker.io/fosrl/newt:1.20.0 The connector image for the exit of each node.

items.title: The order of first setup
items.text:
HomeGAP prepares the cluster in this order:

  1. HomeGAP prepares the mesh and the shared database. The homelab member comes first, then each node.
  2. HomeGAP provisions the nodes one at a time until the Pangolin of the cluster exists. Thus only one node migrates the empty database.
  3. The stack of each node waits until its database member is streaming.

items.title: Users and devices
items.text:
The Access page manages the people who can sign in to the Pangolin apps, and their devices. This page tells you how to use it.

The page is available only in cluster mode. Its subtitle is "Who can sign in to the Pangolin apps, and their devices". You do not sign in to Pangolin as the admin.

items.title: How changes reach Pangolin
items.text:
All nodes share one database. Thus HomeGAP sends each change through the Pangolin of any node that it can reach. The page shows the node, for example "Read through na1's Pangolin". HomeGAP writes each change to the reconcile log.

The first time, HomeGAP gives its API key the permissions that the page needs. This takes one admin login.

items.title: The Pangolin app address
items.text: The Pangolin app address panel shows https://<client_hostname>.<domain>. Click Copy, and give the address to your users. In the Pangolin app, they add it as a self-hosted server. See Connect the Pangolin apps.

items.title: Add a user
items.text:
1. In Add a user, type the email address in Email.
  2. Under Roles, select one or more roles. A new user has the role with the least privilege by default.
  3. Select how the user gets a password. Do one of the procedures below.

The page shows "Pick at least one role" if you do not select a role.

items.title: With a password
items.text:
1. Select Set a password now. The text tells you "They can sign in straight away. Share it with them privately."
  2. In Password, type a password with at least 8 characters.
  3. Click Create user.
  4. Give the password to the user on a private channel.

items.title: With an invite link
items.text:
1. Clear Set a password now.
  2. Click Create invite link. The page shows the Invite link.
  3. Click Copy.
  4. Send the link to the person. The link is valid for 7 days. The person opens it and chooses a password.

items.title: Users
items.text:
The Users panel shows "Everyone who can sign in, on every node".

  • To change the roles of a user, click the role buttons in the Roles column.
  • To remove a user, click Remove. Then confirm. The user can no longer sign in, and the devices of the user stop.

The server admin account that HomeGAP creates has the badge server admin. You cannot remove this user here.

The Open invitations panel shows the invitations that nobody has used yet, with their Expires time. To withdraw an invitation, click Remove.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
The Devices panel shows "Pangolin apps and machine clients, and the node each one relays through". For each device, the table shows:

  • Device: the name of the device.
  • Owner: the email of the person, or Machine client.
  • Status: for example online, offline, blocked or archived.
  • Node: the node that the device relays through.

You can do these actions on a device:

  • Block or Unblock. For Block, the page asks you to confirm.
  • Archive or Restore.
  • Delete. The page asks you to confirm.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Use the names of Pangolin roles in these settings:

  • homegap.roles, for private services, auth=sso and private paths. See the Label reference.
  • cluster.exit_nodes.roles, for the exits. See Exit nodes.

The Admin role can reach everything.

items.title: API
items.text:
The page uses these API routes. See HTTP API.

Route What it does GET /api/access Returns the users, invitations, devices and roles. POST /api/access/users Creates a user, or an invitation. DELETE /api/access/users/{id} Removes a user. PUT /api/access/users/{id}/roles Sets the roles of a user. DELETE /api/access/invitations/{id} Removes an invitation. POST /api/access/devices/{id}/{action} Does an action on a device: block, unblock, archive, unarchive or delete.

items.title: Cluster database
items.text: The cluster database holds the data of the clustered Pangolin. This page tells you how the members elect a primary, how failover and switch-back work, and how to read the Cluster database panel.

items.title: The members
items.text:
The homelab and every node run one member of the database. The containers come from the homegap-cluster image:

Container Nodes Homelab etcd (the vote) Yes Yes (homegap-etcd) PostgreSQL under Patroni Yes Yes (homegap-db) Valkey Yes Yes (homegap-valkey) Valkey Sentinel Yes Yes (homegap-sentinel) HAProxy (cluster-proxy) Yes No The mesh probe Yes No

Thus each node runs five cluster containers plus the probe, and the homelab runs four.

Each node member is its own compose project in /opt/homegap/cluster, under pangolin.install_dir. It is separate from the Pangolin stack, so a stack update never restarts the database. When you remove a node, HomeGAP removes its member from the vote and deletes its data. The Valkey Sentinels never forget a member by themselves. While one still knows a removed member, it uses a full CPU core, so HomeGAP has it forget the member (SENTINEL RESET), one Sentinel at a time and at least 30 seconds apart. The log then shows "Sentinel forgot departed" and the member's address.

items.title: The homelab as a vote only
items.text:
By default, the homelab is a full member. It holds a copy of the database and is the primary when it can.

With cluster.homelab_role: vote, the homelab only votes. It runs etcd and Valkey Sentinel, and it runs no PostgreSQL and no Valkey. The homegap-db and homegap-valkey containers wait and do nothing. The database and Valkey are on the nodes only:

  • The nodes elect the primary between them. The vote of the homelab gives two nodes a majority when one node fails.
  • There is no preferred member and no switch-back. The primary stays where the vote puts it.
  • Once a day, HomeGAP makes a dump of the database on a node. It keeps the newest seven in cluster/backups in the data directory of the orchestrator.
  • homegap maintenance start moves nothing, because the homelab holds no primary.

Each node is a member of the database, and members share their settings. Thus a person with root on a node can run commands in each container that runs a database member. In this mode, no such container is on the homelab. Use it if you do not trust your nodes as much as your homelab. The price is that the live data is on the nodes, not at home.

Caution

Set homelab_role before the first start of the cluster. HomeGAP records the role when it creates the cluster. If you change the value later, the cluster part of each pass fails until you restore the first value.

With this role, use two or more nodes. With one node, the database has no second copy.

items.title: The primary
items.text: The homelab is the primary. It starts the cluster. The nodes then join one at a time: first the vote, then as streaming replicas.

items.title: Failover
items.text:
If the homelab drops off the mesh, the nodes that still reach a majority of the vote promote one of themselves. This takes approximately 30 seconds.

A member that loses the majority demotes itself. This also applies to the homelab, if the homelab is the member that is cut off. Thus two primaries never accept writes at the same time.

The vote needs a majority. To keep the cluster in operation without the homelab, you need two or more nodes.

items.title: Switch-back
items.text: When the homelab comes back, it joins again as a replica. It rewinds the writes that it accepts after the loss of the vote. After the homelab stays caught up for cluster.primary.switch_back_after (default 10 minutes), HomeGAP moves the PostgreSQL primary back to it. Then it moves the Valkey primary.

items.title: Make a member the primary
items.text:
On the Cluster database panel, a caught-up replica has a Make primary button. This is a planned switchover. Writes stop for a second or two, and HomeGAP loses no data. If the new primary is not where the primary belongs, the switch-back returns it after the hold.

The API call is POST /api/cluster/switchover with the body {"to": "<member>"}.

items.title: How services find the primary
items.text:
On each node, the containers on the homegap-cluster Docker network connect to HAProxy:

  • PostgreSQL at cluster-proxy:5433.
  • Valkey at cluster-proxy:6380.

HAProxy follows the current primary. It cuts the connections to a member that demotes itself. The stats page of HAProxy listens only on 127.0.0.1:8404 of the node.

items.title: The cluster-proxy check
items.text:
Each node has a cluster-proxy check. It shows where HAProxy sends PostgreSQL and Valkey. It also shows how many times HAProxy had no primary in the last hour, and the time of the last loss.

State When Red A primary has no member that HAProxy can reach. Yellow For 5 minutes after a loss that HomeGAP did not plan. Green All other times.

A switch that HomeGAP plans also leaves HAProxy without a primary for a moment. Examples are a switch-back, maintenance, a node update and a switch from the dashboard. The check shows "planned switch N min ago", but it stays green.

items.title: Settings, passwords and backups
items.text:
PostgreSQL runs without JIT compilation. Pangolin makes only small lookups, and a connection that uses JIT keeps approximately 40 MB.

A change to the settings does not restart the database. Patroni reads patroni.yml again. The settings that need a restart of PostgreSQL show as pending. The db container of the homelab reads a changed file within ten seconds.

Pangolin uses the database pangolin with the role pangolin, which owns that database and is not a superuser. The homelab member creates both when it creates the cluster. The superuser postgres can sign in only from inside a member. Replication uses the role replicator, and pg_rewind uses the role rewinder.

HomeGAP creates the passwords one time and keeps them in cluster/secrets.json in the data directory. The database keeps the passwords from its creation, so HomeGAP never creates new ones for a cluster that runs. If the file is gone or damaged, the cluster part of each pass fails until you restore the file. Keep a backup of it.

The homelab member writes a nightly pg_dump to ./backups, next to the homelab compose file (HG_BACKUP_DIR: /backups). It keeps the newest seven.

items.title: What to keep
items.text:
A dump holds the database pangolin: the users, the devices, the sites and the resources of Pangolin. To restore a homelab, keep these items together:

  • The dumps in ./backups. With cluster.homelab_role: vote, they are in cluster/backups in the data directory.
  • The data directory of the orchestrator (the homegap-data volume). It holds the state cache, the cluster passwords and the ACME account.
  • The config file.

The dumps are on the same disk as the database of the homelab. We recommend that you copy them to a different machine each day.

Warning

A dump is not encrypted. It contains the email addresses and the password hashes of your Pangolin users. Encrypt each copy that leaves the homelab.

This command makes one encrypted file from the dumps. It reads the passphrase from a file:

tar -cz backups | openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -salt -pass file:backup.pass -out homegap-backups.tar.gz.enc

items.title: Check that a dump restores
items.text:
We recommend that you do this check each month. It restores the newest dump into an empty database and then removes that database. The primary must be on the homelab.

docker compose exec homegap-db sh -c 'gosu postgres createdb -h /var/run/postgresql -U postgres hg_restore_check \
  && gosu postgres pg_restore -h /var/run/postgresql -U postgres --no-owner -d hg_restore_check "$(ls -1t /backups/homegap-*.dump | head -n 1)" \
  && gosu postgres psql -h /var/run/postgresql -U postgres -d hg_restore_check -Atc "select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema = '"'"'public'"'"'"; \
  gosu postgres dropdb -h /var/run/postgresql -U postgres hg_restore_check'

The command prints the number of tables in the dump. A number above zero and no error show that the dump is good.

items.title: Restore a dump
items.text:
Warning

A restore replaces the contents of the database pangolin with the contents of the dump. You lose each change after the time of the dump.

  1. On the dashboard, click Pause. HomeGAP then makes no changes.
  2. In the Cluster database panel, make sure that the primary is on the homelab. If it is not, click Make primary on the homelab member.
  3. On each node, stop Pangolin: 
    docker stop pangolin
  4. On the homelab, restore the dump. Replace the file name: 
    docker compose exec homegap-db gosu postgres pg_restore -h /var/run/postgresql -U postgres --clean --if-exists -d pangolin /backups/homegap-20261101T030000Z.dump
  5. On each node, start Pangolin: 
    docker start pangolin
  6. On the dashboard, click Resume.

The members on the nodes follow the primary. They need no restore.

With cluster.homelab_role: vote, the database is on the nodes. Copy the dump to the node that holds the primary. Then run pg_restore in the db container of that node, in /opt/homegap/cluster, with the same options.

Caution

After a restore, a node that you added after the time of the dump has no site in Pangolin. HomeGAP creates the site again on the next pass, and the tunnel of that node reconnects.

items.title: Maintenance of the homelab member
items.text:
Before you work on the homelab member, move the primaries to the nodes. Run this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap maintenance start

The command does these steps:

  1. If a node updates its own member, the command waits for it, for up to 10 minutes.
  2. It moves the PostgreSQL primary to a node with a planned switchover.
  3. It moves the Valkey primary to a node with a Sentinel failover.
  4. It waits until both primaries are on the nodes.
  5. It holds them there, with no switch-back, until you end maintenance. The hold stops after --minutes N at most (default 30).

To end the hold, run this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap maintenance end

After the end, the usual switch-back applies. deploy/upgrade.sh uses these commands. See Upgrade the homelab.

items.title: Updates of the node members
items.text:
After an upgrade of the homelab, the members on the nodes follow the image of the homelab. HomeGAP pins the image to its registry digest. It updates one node in each pass, and only while every member serves and no maintenance runs.

Each node does these steps:

  1. It pulls the image.
  2. It moves any primary that it holds to the homelab.
  3. It restarts its services one at a time. Each service must serve again before the next one restarts.

The log tells you when and why the update of a node waits.

items.title: The Cluster database panel
items.text:
The Nodes page has a Cluster database panel, with the subtitle "PostgreSQL (Patroni) and Valkey, shared by every node's Pangolin".

The panel shows the PostgreSQL primary, the Valkey primary and the state of the Vote. A banner tells you when a pending switch-back is due. For each member, the table shows:

  • Vote: the etcd state of the member.
  • Database: the PostgreSQL role.
  • Valkey: the Valkey role.
  • Replication lag: how far the replica is behind the primary.

items.title: Alerts
items.text:
The panel shows an alert in these cases:

  • The vote has no majority, or there is no primary. With no majority, the Vote pill tells you "No primary can be elected until enough members are back".
  • A member is cut off from the others, by its mesh handshakes or by its vote.
  • A replica is more than 16 MiB behind the primary.
  • There are fewer than two nodes. Then the cluster cannot elect a primary without the homelab.
  • The state of the EE license.

items.title: Primary history
items.text:
The Primary history table shows each change of the primary and its cause:

Cause Description failover "Elected by the cluster when the primary was lost" switch-back "Moved back by HomeGAP after the hold" maintenance "Moved off the homelab before an upgrade" manual "Switched from the dashboard" first seen "The primary when HomeGAP started recording"

items.title: Failures
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery The node with the primary is down. Sign-ins and changes stop for approximately 30 seconds, while the other members elect a new primary. DNS moves public traffic as for any node. Automatic. The primary returns to the homelab after the hold. The homelab is up, but cut off from the nodes. The homelab loses the vote and stops all writes. The nodes elect a primary and continue to serve. Repair the link. The homelab joins again as a replica and rewinds the writes that it cannot keep. The primary moves back after the hold. The mesh link between two nodes is broken. Nothing is visible while a majority of members still reach each other. The dashboard shows the isolated member. Repair the network. WireGuard connects again by itself. Fewer than half of the members are reachable. The cluster cannot elect a primary. Sign-in and changes fail. Connected apps and public traffic continue to work. Bring the members back. The dashboard shows "no majority".

items.title: Exit nodes
items.text: With exit nodes, the Pangolin apps can send all the traffic of a device through HomeGAP, as a VPN does. This page tells you how to enable the exits and how they work.

items.title: Enable the exits
items.text:
Add cluster.exit_nodes to the config. The person on the device then selects where the traffic leaves for the internet.

cluster:
  exit_nodes:
    nodes: true        # "Exit via <node>" for each node
    homelab: true      # "Exit via homelab"
    roles: [Member]    # who can use them (Admin always can)

items.title: Exit via a node
items.text:
Each node gets a second Pangolin site, exit-<node>. The Newt connector of this site runs on the node itself, in <install_dir>/exit. It uses the host network and talks to the Pangolin of the node on loopback. The image is cluster.exit_nodes.newt_image.

The connector makes the connections of the person from the node. Thus the traffic leaves with the address of that node. This exit continues to work while the homelab is down.

items.title: Exit via homelab
items.text: This is one exit on the homelab site of every node. The device relays through the nearest node, and the connector of the homelab makes the connections. Thus the traffic leaves with your home address. This exit needs the homelab.

items.title: How the exits work
items.text:
The person selects an exit in the Pangolin client. Pangolin calls these exits "exit nodes". While an exit is selected, the default route of the device goes through it.

The exits are Pangolin private resources of the type exit-node: hg-exit-<node> and hg-exit-homelab. They open no new ports. The connector of the node dials out, like all other connectors.

If you disable nodes or homelab, HomeGAP removes those exits. For nodes, it also removes the connector and its site.

The roles in roles can use the exits. The Admin role can always use them.

Pangolin gives the connector of a node the management host of the node as its WireGuard endpoint. HomeGAP sets the address of this host in the compose project of the connector (extra_hosts), with the values of its DNS records. Thus the connector reaches its node, also while public DNS has an old answer.

The DNS servers that the apps can use through the tunnel are also on the exit sites. See DNS through the tunnel.

items.title: Logs
items.text: To see the logs of the exit connector on a node, open the Diagnostics page and select the service newt. See Diagnostics and troubleshooting.

items.title: Cluster mesh
items.text: The cluster mesh is the private network of the cluster. This page tells you how the mesh works and how to read the Cluster mesh panel.

items.title: What the mesh is
items.text:
hg-mesh is a private WireGuard mesh between the homelab and every node. Cluster traffic uses only this mesh: the database, Valkey and the node API of Gerbil.

The addresses are fixed. The homelab is host 1 of cluster.mesh.subnet. A node is host 10 + slot, where the slot is the permanent tunnel slot of the node. With the default subnet, the homelab is 10.77.0.1 and the first node is 10.77.0.10.

items.title: Keys and connections
items.text:
Each node creates its own key during its first setup. The private key stays on the node. HomeGAP knows only the public key.

The homelab can be behind NAT. It dials every node and keeps the paths open, so HomeGAP never publishes its address. The nodes connect to each other directly on their public addresses.

The firewall of each node opens cluster.mesh.port/udp to anywhere. WireGuard authenticates every packet, and the address of the homelab can change. On the mesh interface, the firewall accepts only the ports of the cluster services. A member cannot reach SSH or other ports of a node through the mesh.

On the homelab end of the mesh, HomeGAP drops inbound traffic, except replies, ping and the ports of the cluster database. Thus the nodes reach only the cluster services of the homelab.

items.title: The interfaces
items.text:
On each node, wg-quick manages the interface, and it starts at boot. Changes to the peers apply in place. They do not drop the sessions.

On the homelab, the interface is in the network namespace of the homegap-mesh container. The cluster containers of the homelab share this namespace. The orchestrator is not in it. deploy/upgrade.sh never recreates homegap-mesh, so the interface stays up during an upgrade.

The homegap-mesh-agent container manages the interface. The orchestrator writes the description of the mesh to the homegap-mesh volume. The agent applies it. Then it writes its public key and the state of each peer to the same volume. The private key of the homelab stays in that volume.

items.title: The isolation of the homelab member
items.text:
Each node is a member of the cluster database, so HomeGAP treats the namespace of homegap-mesh as reachable from the nodes. The agent keeps a firewall there that refuses everything except these connections:

  • Into the namespace: replies, ping and the ports of the cluster database.
  • Out of the namespace: the mesh, replies and WireGuard to the nodes.
  • Through the namespace: the orchestrator to the members on the mesh, and the replies.

Thus a container in that namespace cannot open a connection to the orchestrator, to your other containers or to your home network. The agent installs the firewall before it starts the interface. If the firewall fails, the mesh stays down.

The orchestrator reaches the members through this namespace. It adds a route for cluster.mesh.subnet through homegap-mesh on the homegap-cluster network. For that route it needs NET_ADMIN.

items.title: What a container on a node can reach
items.text:
Pangolin on a node faces the internet. HomeGAP keeps the containers of a node away from the services that control the cluster:

  • The firewall of the node admits the containers only to PostgreSQL, Valkey and the health check of Patroni on the member of their own node.
  • A forward rule in the DOCKER-USER chain drops packets from a container to two ports of another member. The ports are the etcd peer port (2380) and the Sentinel port (26379). Docker forwards a container to the mesh as the node itself, so the other member sees no difference between them. The rule is on the node that sends. wg-quick adds it again at boot.
  • etcd needs a password. The etcd client port (2379) stays reachable for the probe of HAProxy, but each read and each write needs the etcd root user. Only the members and the orchestrator hold that password.
  • Sentinel needs a password. It is not the Valkey password, which Pangolin holds.

A person with root on a node holds these passwords, because the member of that node needs them. See Security model.

items.title: Probes
items.text:
Once a second, each node opens a TCP connection to the etcd port of every other member. It does this on two paths:

  • From the host, like etcd, Patroni and replication. A small probe container in the cluster member of the node does this on the host network. The node keeps the readings in /run/homegap-probe, so a reboot clears them.
  • From inside the Docker network, through the checks of HAProxy. This is the path of the database and Valkey traffic of Pangolin, across the homegap-cluster bridge and its NAT.

The homelab does not send probes, but every node sends probes to it.

items.title: The Cluster mesh panel
items.text:
The Nodes page has a Cluster mesh panel. For each node and peer, it shows Host probe (last hour) and Container probe (last hour). Each probe column shows:

  • The latest round trip.
  • The part of the probes lost in the last hour.
  • Each outage, with its start and its duration. An outage is three or more lost probes in a row.

A degraded pill means some loss or an outage in the last hour. A red pill means that the peer does not answer now. If only the container column shows a problem, the link is good. The problem is then in the Docker network of that node.

The Last handshake with column shows a pill for each peer, with the peer and the time since the last WireGuard handshake. The color and the description of the pill tell the state:

Pill Description Meaning Green None. The last handshake is 3 minutes old or less. Yellow "No recent handshake" The last handshake is 3 to 10 minutes old. Red "No handshake for over 10 minutes" The last handshake is more than 10 minutes old. Red, never "No handshake yet" The member has never had a handshake with the peer. Red, not configured "Not in this member's peer list yet" The member does not have this peer in its configuration yet.

items.title: Connect the Pangolin apps
items.text: The Pangolin app (by Fossorial) connects a device to your private services. This page tells you which address to use and how to connect a device.

items.title: The server address
items.text:
ClusterStandalone

The server address is https://pangolin.<domain>. The Access page shows it as the Pangolin app address. Every node serves this address, and DNS sends each device to the nearest healthy node. The app selects the node when it connects or when it changes network.

Each node has its own Pangolin and its own users. The app connects to the management host of one node, https://pangolin-<id>.<domain>.

items.title: Connect a device
items.text:
1. Add the person on the Access page, with a password or an invite link. See Users and devices.
  2. If the person has an invite link, the person opens it and chooses a password.
  3. The person installs the Pangolin app for their platform: Android, iOS, macOS, Linux, Windows, CLI
  4. In the app, the person adds a self-hosted server and types the server address.
  1. The person signs in with the email address and the password.
  1. The person connects the app.
  1. On the Access page, find the device in the Devices list. Make sure that it shows as online, with the node that it relays through.
  2. Optional: if exit nodes are enabled, the person selects an exit in the app. See Exit nodes.

items.title: What the app reaches
items.text:
A connected app reaches these services:

  • The private services, by their hostnames. See Private services.
  • The private paths of public services. See Client addresses and private-only services.

items.title: DNS through the tunnel
items.text:
The Pangolin app has the setting DNS over tunnel. With this setting, the app sends its DNS queries through the tunnel to its upstream DNS server. The default upstream server of the app is 8.8.8.8. The app can send queries only to a server that is a Pangolin resource. Without such a resource, the app resolves only the names of your private services, and other sites do not open.

HomeGAP makes each server in cluster.tunnel_dns.resolvers a private resource, hg-dns-<address>, on port 53 (TCP and UDP). The default is 8.8.8.8, the default of the app, so the app needs no change. The roles in cluster.tunnel_dns.roles can use it.

  • If cluster.exit_nodes.nodes is enabled, the resource is on the exit site of each node. The queries leave from the node that the device uses, the nearest node. Thus geo-steered names resolve to locations near the device.
  • If not, the resource is on the homelab site of each node. The queries leave from your homelab.

The resource works without an exit node. If you set another upstream server in the app, add its address to cluster.tunnel_dns.resolvers.

items.title: While the homelab is down
items.text: The apps that are connected stay connected. New sign-ins work approximately 30 seconds later, when the nodes elect a database primary. Only the services on the homelab are not reachable.

items.title: Clustered Pangolin
items.text: In cluster mode, the Pangolin of each node is one instance of a single Pangolin EE cluster. This page tells you how the instances share the work.

items.title: The image
items.text: Each node runs the PostgreSQL build of the configured image. The tag ee-<version> becomes ee-postgresql-<version>. The default of pangolin.pangolin_image is docker.io/fosrl/pangolin:ee-1.26.0.

items.title: Reads and writes
items.text: Pangolin sends writes to the current primary through cluster-proxy. It reads from the database member on its own node. A sign-in, and the use of the session at once, works through a node approximately 300 ms from the primary. The end-to-end tests check this with added latency on the mesh.

items.title: Sites and resources
items.text:
Each node is its own region. The homelab gets one site for each node, with the name <site_name>-<node id>, for example homelab-na1. HomeGAP creates each site through its node. Thus the connector of the site always uses the exit node of that node.

Each service is one resource with a target on the site of every node. HomeGAP applies the resources one time in each pass, through the first node that is ready. A node routes only through its own target. Thus every node keeps its own tunnel to the homelab, and no node relays through another node.

Some things stay separate on each node:

  • The private resources list the site of every node that serves them. A client uses the nearest node when it connects.
  • Each node has its own health resource, hg-health-<node id>, and its own speed test host.
  • The passthrough ports are the same on every node.

DNS sends a hostname only to a node that has its own target for it.

Traefik reads the routes of Pangolin from a file (traefik.file_mode). Each node writes this file for its own sites. The passthrough routes of HomeGAP are in the same directory.

items.title: The client address
items.text:
The clients use one address, <client_hostname>.<domain> (default pangolin.<domain>). Every node serves the login pages and the API of Pangolin on this address. A geo record with a health monitor sends it to the nearest healthy node. Thus sign-in and device enrollment work while the homelab is down.

Passthrough never captures this address.

items.title: Gerbil
items.text: The API of Gerbil is available only over the mesh, on the mesh address of the node. Thus the other Pangolin instances of the cluster can reach it. Docker starts after the mesh interface.

items.title: One admin, one API key, one license
items.text:
The first node creates the admin, the org and the API key of the cluster. HomeGAP keeps the admin and the server secret in the state of the orchestrator and on every node. Thus you can recover them from any node.

HomeGAP activates pangolin.license_key_env one time, through the first node that can activate it. Then it tells the other nodes to read the license again. HomeGAP ignores a license_key_env on a node. See Pangolin EE licenses.

items.title: Upgrades
items.text: HomeGAP updates the nodes one at a time. The first node that starts a new Pangolin version migrates the database. Before this, it saves a dump of the database. If that update fails, the rollback also restores the dump. See Node updates and rollback.

items.title: Removal of a node
items.text:
When you decommission a node, HomeGAP also removes what the node left in the Pangolin of the cluster, on the next pass:

  • The homelab site of the node.
  • The exit site of the node.
  • The exit node that its Gerbil registered. HomeGAP finds it by its region, which is the node id.

HomeGAP removes the leftovers of nodes from earlier removals in the same way. See Manage nodes.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: HomeGAP reads its configuration from one YAML file. This page tells you where the file is, when changes apply and how HomeGAP checks the file.

items.title: The file
items.text:
The orchestrator finds the file in this order:

  1. The --config PATH option.
  2. The HOMEGAP_CONFIG environment variable.
  3. The default path, /config/config.yml.

The repository has a complete example in config/config.example.yml. For every key, see the Configuration reference.

The parser is strict. An unknown key is an error.

items.title: A minimal config
items.text:
domain: example.net
bunny:
  zone: example.net
pangolin:
  acme_email: ops@example.net
nodes: []
dashboard:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:8088

items.title: When changes apply
items.text:
The orchestrator reads the file again on each pass. Thus most edits apply without a restart. If an edit is not valid, the orchestrator writes the error to the log, and the last good configuration stays in effect.

These changes need a restart of the orchestrator:

  • A change of speedtest.enabled or speedtest.bind.
  • The first activation of the status page (status_page.enabled).
  • A change of the dashboard token. The orchestrator reads the token one time, at the start.
  • A change of dashboard.bind.

items.title: Check the file
items.text:
To check the file, run homegap validate. In the container, use this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap validate

To check a different file, add --config PATH. If the file is valid, the command prints OK: <n> node(s), domain <domain>, zone <zone>. If not, it prints Invalid configuration: and the list of errors.

items.title: Edits from the dashboard
items.text:
With dashboard.allow_config_edits: true (the default), the dashboard can add and remove nodes. Each such change writes the config file again. The config mount must be writable for this.

Each change from the dashboard starts from the file on the disk. Thus an edit that you make by hand a moment before stays in the file. If the file has an error, HomeGAP does not write it, and the dashboard shows the error.

Before each write, HomeGAP saves the previous file next to it as <file>.bak-<epoch ms>, with mode 0600. It keeps the newest 10 backups. The new file starts with this comment:

# Managed by HomeGAP; edited from the dashboard. Previous version saved alongside as .bak-*

Caution

The new file contains only the values that are different from the defaults. If you edit nodes on the dashboard, HomeGAP does not keep the comments of your file. Keep a copy of your commented file if you need it.

items.title: Durations
items.text: A duration is a number with a unit: ms, s, m or h. A number without a unit is in seconds. Examples are 60s, 5m and 2h.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text:
homegap validate and each read of the file check these rules:

  • domain is a plain hostname, without a leading dot and without *.
  • bunny.zone is equal to domain, or a parent of it.
  • bunny.routing is geolocation, latency or none.
  • bunny.monitor is http, ping or none.
  • acme.directory starts with https://.
  • Each node id matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$, and each node id is unique.
  • Each ssh_allow_from entry is an IP address or a CIDR.
  • Each node has an IPv4 address (public_ipv4, or a host that is an IPv4 literal), or a public_ipv6.
  • With geolocation routing, each node has a location or a known region code.
  • With latency routing, each node has a latency_zone.
  • reconcile.resync_interval, reconcile.debounce and reconcile.node_check_interval are valid durations.
  • tunnels.mtu is from 1280 to 1500.
  • dashboard.bind is in the form host:port.

When the status page is enabled:

  • status_page.hostname is a single lowercase label that matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9]{0,20}$.
  • status_page.hostname is different from speedtest.hostname, if the speed test is also enabled.
  • status_page.title has 60 characters or fewer.
  • speedtest.bind is in the form host:port, and it is different from dashboard.bind.

When the speed test is enabled:

  • speedtest.hostname is a single lowercase label.
  • speedtest.phase_seconds is from 2 to 30.
  • speedtest.link_budget_gb is from 1 to 1000.
  • speedtest.streams is from 1 to 16.
  • speedtest.link_ttl is a valid duration, and speedtest.bind is in the form host:port.
  • speedtest.bind is different from dashboard.bind.

In cluster mode:

  • cluster.mesh.subnet is a valid subnet. It does not overlap 100.64.0.0/10.
  • cluster.mesh.subnet has space for 32 nodes (/26 or larger).
  • cluster.mesh.port is from 1 to 65535, and it is not 51820 or 21820.
  • cluster.primary.preferred is homelab.
  • cluster.primary.switch_back_after is a valid duration.
  • cluster.image is not empty.

items.title: Certificates
items.text: A node holds a certificate only for a name that it terminates. This page tells you which names those are, how HomeGAP orders the certificate, and why a node cannot get other certificates.

items.title: The risk of a certificate on a node
items.text:
A browser accepts each valid certificate for a name. All traffic to your domain goes through a node. Thus a person with root on a node can read the traffic of each name on the certificate of that node. That person ends TLS on the node, reads or changes the request, and sends the request to the homelab. The browser and the homelab see no difference.

For this reason, HomeGAP gives a node no certificate for a passthrough name.

items.title: Which names are on the certificate
items.text:
Name On the certificate of the nodes The management host of each node, pangolin-<id>.<domain>. Yes. In cluster mode, the client address pangolin.<domain>. Yes. The shared names of the status page and the speed test. Yes. A service with homegap.tls: terminate. Yes. A service with homegap.tls: passthrough. No. The front door with passthrough, with or without homegap.wildcard. No. The front door with terminate. Yes: the root name, and *.<domain> if the front door has homegap.wildcard.

The activity log shows each order, with the number of names. An order can take some minutes, because it waits for DNS. The reconcile pass does not wait for the order. When the order is complete, the next pass gives the new certificate to the nodes.

items.title: The front door in terminate mode with a wildcard
items.text:
This is the only setup that puts a wildcard certificate on the nodes. The nodes then end TLS for each name one label under your domain. A person with root on a node can read all of that traffic.

Warning

With homegap.tls: terminate and homegap.wildcard: "true" on the front door, the nodes hold a certificate for *.<domain>. Use this setup only if you trust each node and its provider with all web traffic of the domain.

In this setup, HomeGAP refuses a service with homegap.tls: passthrough on a hostname one label under the domain. The wildcard on the nodes covers that hostname, so passthrough protects nothing. The error is homegap.tls=passthrough is refused for <hostname>. Set homegap.tls: terminate on that service, or use passthrough on the front door.

HomeGAP does not refuse a raw TCP or UDP service. A certificate has no effect on a protocol that does not use TLS. But a raw TCP service that uses TLS for a name under the domain has the same risk as a web service.

items.title: How HomeGAP orders the certificate
items.text:
The orchestrator on the homelab orders one certificate from Let's Encrypt. The certificate lists each name from the table above. Each node gets the same certificate and the same key.

HomeGAP uses the DNS challenge:

  1. The orchestrator starts Lego, an ACME client in the homegap image.
  2. For each name, Lego asks the orchestrator for a TXT record _acme-challenge.<name>. Lego calls an endpoint on the loopback address of the orchestrator.
  3. The orchestrator writes the record with its own Bunny client. Lego never gets the Bunny key.
  4. Let's Encrypt reads the records and issues the certificate.
  5. The orchestrator removes the records and sends the certificate to each node.

A node orders no certificate. The Traefik on a node has no certificate resolver.

HomeGAP orders a new certificate, with a new key, in these cases:

  • The list of names changes.
  • One third of the lifetime of the certificate remains.
  • The ACME directory in the config changes.

If a name leaves the list, HomeGAP also revokes the old certificate, because the nodes have its key. This occurs when you remove a node, or when you change a service from terminate to passthrough.

A new certificate does not restart the stack of a node. Traefik loads it in a few seconds.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• One certificate has at most 100 names. With more names, the order fails, and the activity log shows the error.
  • Let's Encrypt has a limit of approximately 50 new certificates for a domain in a week. HomeGAP uses one for each change of the list of names.

items.title: The CAA records
items.text:
HomeGAP publishes two CAA records for domain, with the tags issue and issuewild. Each has this value:

letsencrypt.org; validationmethods=dns-01

With these records, only Let's Encrypt can issue a certificate for the domain, and only with the DNS challenge. A node has no DNS key. Thus a compromised node cannot order a certificate for one of your names, although the traffic for that name goes through it.

HomeGAP removes other CAA records for domain, because they can give more permissions.

Caution

The CAA records also apply to the Traefik of your homelab. It must order its certificates from Let's Encrypt with the DNS challenge. If it uses a different certificate authority or a different challenge, its renewals fail. In that case, set acme.caa: false, or set acme.caa_issuer to the CAA name of your certificate authority.

items.title: Config
items.text:
acme:
  email: ops@example.net
Key Default What it does email pangolin.acme_email, then the admin email. The contact address of the ACME account. staging false Uses the staging directory of Let's Encrypt. Browsers do not trust its certificates. Use it for tests. directory The directory of Let's Encrypt. The address of a different ACME directory. caa true Publishes the CAA records. caa_issuer letsencrypt.org The certificate authority in the CAA records.

items.title: Where HomeGAP keeps the certificate
items.text:
The ACME account key, the certificate and its key are in acme/ in the data directory of the orchestrator. Include this folder in your backup of the data directory. If you lose it, HomeGAP makes a new account and orders a new certificate.

On a node, the certificate is config/traefik/certs/homegap.crt and the key is homegap.key, with mode 0600.

items.title: Expiry and failures
items.text:
The Nodes page on the dashboard shows the expiry of the certificate on each node.

If an order fails, the nodes keep the certificate that they have. HomeGAP writes the error in the activity log and tries again after one hour. A node without a certificate answers its names with the default certificate of Traefik, and browsers show a warning.

These are possible causes of a failed order:

  • The Bunny API key is not set, or it cannot change the zone.
  • The homelab cannot reach Let's Encrypt.
  • A CAA record that HomeGAP does not manage, on a name above domain, refuses Let's Encrypt.

items.title: DNS routing and health checks
items.text: Bunny DNS sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. This page tells you how to configure the routing and the monitors, which records HomeGAP creates and how failover works.

items.title: Routing
items.text:
bunny.routing selects how Bunny chooses a node:

Value How Bunny chooses geolocation (default) By the location (latitude and longitude) of each node. If a node has only a region, HomeGAP uses the center of the region. latency By the Bunny latency zones. Each node needs a latency_zone. none No smart routing. The records are plain records.

bunny.ttl sets the TTL of the records (default 60 seconds).

items.title: Monitors
items.text:
bunny.monitor sets the monitor on each geo record:

  • http (we recommend it). Bunny sends a request to http://<node-ip>/. The node sends the request through the tunnel to the health path of the front door.
  • ping.
  • none.

The records for the management hosts, the speed test of each node and the status page of each node have no monitor.

The health path is the homegap.healthcheck of the front door (default /). Bunny sends a probe every 30 seconds from three regions. If the origin is down, the probe gets a 502. If the tunnel is down, the probe fails within 5 seconds.

items.title: Failover
items.text:
Bunny removes the offline members from a record set. The next-nearest node then answers. If all members are offline, Bunny returns all of them (fail-open).

In practice, failover takes approximately 1 to 5 minutes: the health interval, plus the TTL, plus the time that resolvers cache the answer.

Note

A single record cannot fail over. With one node, Bunny continues to answer with that node when it is down.

items.title: The records
items.text:
Name Purpose Type of record <domain> root A geo record set. *.<domain> wildcard A geo record set, only with homegap.wildcard. Each public dedicated hostname service:<key> One geo record set for each hostname, also when several raw services share it. The key is the key of the first service. pangolin.<domain> client In cluster mode, a geo record set with all nodes. speedtest.<domain> speedtest A geo record set, only without a wildcard. speedtest-<node>.<domain> speedtest A plain record for each node. status.<domain> status A geo record set, also with a wildcard. status-<node>.<domain> status A plain record for each node. pangolin-<node>.<domain> management A plain record for each node.

HomeGAP creates A records, and AAAA records for nodes with public_ipv6.

A record set includes only the nodes that serve the service (homegap.regions). For a shared hostname, it includes every node that serves any of its services. If a node refuses the wildcard (terminate without EE), HomeGAP leaves it out of the wildcard set. When you remove a node, HomeGAP first removes it from DNS.

items.title: Ownership of records
items.text:
HomeGAP marks each of its records with the comment managed-by:homegap <purpose> node=<id>. It does not touch records that it did not create, except at the names that it manages.

Warning

At a name that HomeGAP manages, HomeGAP deletes some records that it did not create. The log and the Config diff give the reason "collides with a managed record set".

  • HomeGAP deletes an A or AAAA record with the same name and type as a managed record.
  • HomeGAP deletes any CNAME record at that name.
  • HomeGAP adopts a record that has exactly the desired value.

Before you disable dry run, look for delete rows in the diff on the Config page.

HomeGAP keeps the records of paused nodes and paused services as they are.

items.title: Reads of the zone
items.text: When the desired records do not change, HomeGAP reads the whole zone again every reconcile.dns_check_interval (default 5 minutes). Thus it finds edits from the Bunny console. A change to the desired records syncs at once.

items.title: The DNS page
items.text: The DNS page on the dashboard shows the records, the state of their monitors and if they match the desired state.

items.title: Pangolin EE licenses
items.text: Most of HomeGAP works with plain Pangolin. Two features need Pangolin EE. This page tells you when you need an EE license key and how to give it to HomeGAP in each mode.

items.title: When you need a license
items.text:
• Cluster mode. The nodes run as one Pangolin EE cluster, and one key covers all of them.
  • Wildcard HTTP resources in terminate mode, where the nodes end TLS. For example, the front door with homegap.tls: terminate.

Other EE features that you use yourself also need a key, for example shared policies in a base blueprint. Standalone nodes that pass TLS through to the homelab need no license.

Pangolin EE has its own license terms. It is free for personal use and for organizations below its commercial revenue threshold.

items.title: Keys bind to one instance
items.text:
A key binds to one Pangolin instance when you activate it the first time. If a second instance tries the same key, the license server refuses it with "already been activated with a different instance name".

Warning

The license server records each activation. Do not activate production keys on test instances or on instances that you discard later.

items.title: The key in each mode
items.text:
ClusterStandalone

One key covers every node, because all nodes share one database. Set pangolin.license_key_env, or pangolin.license_key_file.

HomeGAP activates the key through the first node that can activate it. Then it tells the other nodes to read it again. HomeGAP ignores the keys of single nodes. The Cluster database panel shows the state of the license.

Each node needs its own key. Set nodes[].license_key_env for each node. pangolin.license_key_env is only a default, for a setup with one node.

If a node refuses a key, HomeGAP reports it one time for that node, in the dashboard check ee-license. HomeGAP does not try the key again until the key changes.

items.title: Give the keys to the orchestrator
items.text:
Put the keys in .env, and give the variables to the orchestrator in the compose file. For example, in standalone mode with two nodes:

services:
  orchestrator:
    environment:
      PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA1: ${PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA1}
      PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA2: ${PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA2}

nodes:
  - id: na1
    license_key_env: PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA1
  - id: na2
    license_key_env: PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY_NA2

The node entries above show only the license key. A real node entry also needs host and ssh_key_file. See Secrets.

items.title: Pangolin options
items.text: The pangolin section controls the stack that HomeGAP installs on each node. This page tells you what the options do. For the defaults, see the Configuration reference.

items.title: Images
items.text:
These keys set the images of the node stack:

  • pangolin_image
  • gerbil_image
  • traefik_image
  • maintenance_image
  • crowdsec_image

A change of an image changes the node stack. Thus HomeGAP updates the nodes one at a time, with rollback. See Node updates and rollback.

In cluster mode, HomeGAP changes the Pangolin tag to the PostgreSQL build: ee-<version> becomes ee-postgresql-<version>.

badger_version sets the version of Badger, the Traefik plugin of Pangolin.

items.title: Names
items.text:
HomeGAP gives these names to the objects that it creates:

Key Object org_id The id of the Pangolin org. org_name The name of the Pangolin org. admin_email The email of the admin account. site_name The name of the homelab site. In cluster mode, each node gets <site_name>-<node id>.

HomeGAP creates the admin account without a person at the keyboard. It does this on each node, or one time for the cluster.

items.title: The install directory
items.text:
install_dir (default /opt/homegap) is the directory of the stack on each node. It holds:

  • The compose file and config/.
  • secrets/node.json, the secrets of the node.
  • .homegap-rollback, the saved stack for a rollback.
  • cluster/, the cluster member, in cluster mode.
  • exit/, the exit connector, if exits through nodes are enabled.

items.title: The base blueprint
items.text:
base_blueprint names a Pangolin blueprint, in YAML or JSON. HomeGAP applies it to every node before the managed resources. In cluster mode, it applies it one time for the cluster. When the content of the file changes, HomeGAP applies it again.

Use the base blueprint for static configuration that does not come from labels, for example shared resource policies. Shared policies are an EE feature.

Caution

Keys in the base blueprint must not start with hg-. HomeGAP reserves this prefix for the resources that it manages, and it can delete them.

This example comes from blueprints/base.example.yml. Mount the file and set pangolin.base_blueprint: /config/blueprints/base.yml:

public-policies:
  allow-everyone:
    name: allow-everyone
    rules:
      - action: allow
        match: cidr
        value: 0.0.0.0/0
        priority: 1000

For the blueprint format, see the Pangolin blueprint reference.

items.title: CrowdSec
items.text:
crowdsec: true enables the CrowdSec bouncer on the Traefik of each node. It uses crowdsec_image and crowdsec_bouncer_version. CrowdSec protects only terminated traffic. It cannot examine passthrough streams.

If a node cannot reach the AppSec component of CrowdSec, it lets the requests through. With crowdsec_fail_closed: true, the node refuses them. Then a stopped CrowdSec container stops the terminated traffic of that node, and its own Pangolin pages too.

items.title: Ports and tuning
items.text:
passthrough_port_base (default 40000) is the start of the internal proxy ports for passthrough resources. HomeGAP never publishes these ports.

tcp_tuning (default true) applies TCP tuning on each node. See Performance.

items.title: Managed and unmanaged objects
items.text: HomeGAP deletes only stale hg-* resources. The resources that you create by hand in the Pangolin of a node stay.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: The config file never holds a secret. This page tells you how to give secrets to the orchestrator, and where HomeGAP keeps the secrets that it creates.

items.title: References to secrets
items.text:
Each secret in the config is a reference:

  • A key that ends in _env names an environment variable.
  • A key that ends in _file names a file that you mount in the container.

For each secret, HomeGAP tries these sources in this order:

  1. The environment variable, if it is set and not blank.
  2. The file, if it is set and not blank.
  3. The file /run/secrets/<ENV_NAME>, with the name from the *_env key. This is the convention of Docker secrets.

HomeGAP removes spaces and line breaks at the start and the end of each value.

items.title: The secrets that the config references
items.text:
The Config page on the dashboard lists each secret that the config references, and shows if it is present or missing. The page never shows the values. The list contains:

  • The Bunny DNS API key.
  • The Pangolin EE license for all nodes, if you set one.
  • The bearer token of the dashboard, if you set one.
  • For each node, the SSH key (ssh_key_file), and the license of the node if you set one.

The PINs of homegap.pin_env are also secrets. HomeGAP reads them for each service. See Pangolin sign-in for services.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Put the values in .env next to the compose file. Use mode 600, and never commit the file.

BUNNY_API_KEY=...
PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY=...
HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN=...

Then give the variables to the orchestrator in the compose file:

services:
  orchestrator:
    environment:
      BUNNY_API_KEY: ${BUNNY_API_KEY:?set BUNNY_API_KEY}
      PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY: ${PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY:-}
      HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN: ${HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN}

The config refers to the variables by their names:

bunny:
  api_key_env: BUNNY_API_KEY
pangolin:
  license_key_env: PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY
dashboard:
  auth_token_env: HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN

items.title: Docker secrets
items.text:
Docker mounts each secret at /run/secrets/<name>. If the name of the secret is the same as the name in the *_env key, HomeGAP finds it there:

services:
  orchestrator:
    secrets: [BUNNY_API_KEY]

secrets:
  BUNNY_API_KEY:
    file: ./secrets/bunny_api_key

With bunny.api_key_env: BUNNY_API_KEY and no BUNNY_API_KEY variable, HomeGAP reads /run/secrets/BUNNY_API_KEY.

items.title: Secrets that HomeGAP creates
items.text:
HomeGAP creates some secrets itself:

  • The secrets of each node: the Pangolin server secret, the admin credentials, the setup token and the CrowdSec bouncer key. They come from the CSPRNG of the kernel. HomeGAP sends them over SSH to <install_dir>/secrets/node.json on the node, with mode 0600.
  • The cluster passwords, in cluster/secrets.json in the data directory. HomeGAP creates them one time and never replaces them. Keep a backup of this file.
  • The dashboard token, in dashboard-token in the data directory, if the config gives none.
  • The SSH keys that the add-node wizard generates, in <data dir>/ssh/, with mode 0600.

The file node.json on the node is the source of truth. The local state file /data/state.json (mode 0600) is only a cache. If you lose it, HomeGAP reads the credentials from the nodes again.

For the full security model, see Security model.

items.title: Build from source
items.text: This page tells you how to build and test HomeGAP, how CI builds the image, and how to contribute.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: You need JDK 21. The build downloads Gradle, Kotlin/Native and Node (for the dashboard) by itself.

items.title: Commands
items.text: Command What it does ./gradlew macosArm64Test Runs the unit tests on the host target. ./gradlew :presentation:jsNodeTest Runs the presenter tests of the dashboard, on Node. ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64 Builds the two Linux binaries. ./gradlew -Phomegap.skipWeb=true … Skips the dashboard bundle, for fast iteration. ./gradlew :web:jsBrowserDevelopmentServe --continuous Runs the development server of the dashboard. It sends /api to port 8088. tools/build-map.sh tiles Builds map/world.pmtiles for local runs. The image builds its own tiles.

items.title: The image
items.text:
The image build needs the two Linux binaries first:

  1. Build the binaries: 
    ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64
  2. Build the image: 
    docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t homegap .

The Dockerfile builds the map tiles and these docs (mkdocs.embedded.yml) itself.

items.title: CI
items.text:
.github/workflows/build.yml runs on pushes to main, on version tags and on pull requests. It runs the unit tests and the presenter tests, then builds the multi-arch image. On pushes to main and on version tags, it publishes the image to GHCR. The image tags are:

Event Tags A push to main main, sha-<short> A tag vX.Y.Z X.Y.Z, X.Y, latest

items.title: Repository layout
items.text:
src/nativeMain/kotlin/homegap/
  discovery/    Docker socket client + label parsing
  model/        pure planner: labels + config -> desired state
  reconcile/    controller loop and the node, tunnel, resource and DNS reconcilers
  clients/      Pangolin (integration + bootstrap), Bunny, SSH (OpenSSH ControlMaster)
  provision/    node stack templates, certificates, YAML emitter
  state/        local state cache
  dashboard/    REST API + embedded SPA, and the map's files
  locations/    the locations catalog (shipped list + local edits)
  tunnels/      Newt connector supervisor
api/            wire types shared by the API and the dashboard
web/            Compose for HTML dashboard, bundled with Vite (kotlin-vite)
deploy/         homelab compose; reference node stack
blueprints/     example Pangolin base blueprint
config/         example configuration
locations/      the shipped data-center catalog (datacenters.yml)
tools/          build-map.sh: the self-hosted map's tiles
e2e/            end-to-end harness

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Issues and pull requests are welcome. Before you open a pull request, make sure that the unit tests pass (./gradlew macosArm64Test). For changes to provisioning, routing or DNS, the end-to-end harness must also pass. See End-to-end tests.

For changes to these docs, see Documentation.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: These docs are built with Zensical, from the Material for MkDocs team. Zensical reads mkdocs.yml. This page tells you how to preview and build them, how the versions work and where the dashboard copy comes from.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
• The config is mkdocs.yml.
  • The pages are in docs/.
  • docs/requirements.txt pins the dependencies: zensical 0.1.0, pymdown-extensions 13.0, and the Zensical fork of mike (tag 2.2.0+zensical-0.1.0). The fork is not on PyPI. pip installs it from GitHub, so git must be installed.

The theme is dark (slate), and it uses system fonts. The site loads no fonts from a third party.

items.title: Preview the docs
items.text:
1. Install the dependencies: 
    python3 -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
  2. Start the preview server: 
    zensical serve
  3. Open http://localhost:8000.

To build the site as CI does, run a strict build. A broken link or a missing page fails it.

zensical build --strict

The output goes to site/.

items.title: Variables and Jinja
items.text:
Every page goes through Jinja, through Zensical's own version of the markdownextradata plugin. The variable hg_version gives the version that the pages describe. It comes from the VERSION environment variable, with the default dev.

Caution

Literal Jinja delimiters in a page, for example in a Go template for docker inspect, break the build. Put such text in a Jinja raw block.

items.title: Versions
items.text:
.github/workflows/docs.yml builds both configs on every push and pull request that changes the docs. It publishes to GitHub Pages (the gh-pages branch) with the Zensical fork of mike, but only when the repository is public:

Event Version A push to main dev A tag vX.Y.Z X.Y, with the alias latest. latest becomes the default.

items.title: The copy in the image
items.text:
The Dockerfile builds mkdocs.embedded.yml into /usr/share/homegap/docs. This config inherits mkdocs.yml, but it has no version selector and no mike. The image build gives it VERSION, and build.yml passes the image version. The image build does not install mike.

The dashboard serves this copy at /docs/, and links it as Documentation at the bottom of the sidebar. To use a different folder, set HOMEGAP_DOCS_DIR. For example, build a local copy and point the orchestrator at it:

zensical build -f mkdocs.embedded.yml

The output goes to site-embedded/.

items.title: Writing rules
items.text:
Follow the Writing style guide for every page.

A screenshot that the maintainer must add is an HTML comment on its own line, in this form:

<!-- SCREENSHOT: docs/img/<page>/<nn>-<what>.png | what the image shows -->

The images go in docs/img/.

Do not use Mermaid diagrams. Mermaid loads from a CDN, and the copy on the dashboard must work without internet access.

items.title: End-to-end tests
items.text: The e2e/ folder has a self-contained end-to-end harness. This page tells you what the harness contains, how to run it and what it checks.

items.title: The harness
items.text:
The harness has these parts:

  • A fake Ubuntu VPS, with sshd and its own Docker daemon.
  • A simulated homelab, with Traefik, whoami and socat.
  • The orchestrator and the tunnel supervisor.
  • A stand-in for the Bunny API.

items.title: Run the harness
items.text:
1. Build the Linux binary for your Docker host. On an amd64 host, use linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 instead. 
    ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64
  2. Start the harness. It provisions two fake nodes from nothing, over SSH. 
    e2e/run.sh
  3. Run the checks of the data plane: 
    e2e/verify.sh

To test EE features, put the keys, for example PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY, in an untracked .env file at the root of the repository. e2e/run.sh exports it.

The dashboard of the harness is at http://127.0.0.1:18088.

items.title: What verify.sh checks
items.text:
e2e/verify.sh does these checks on every node:

  • Passthrough of the root, with the certificate of the origin.
  • The address of the viewer at the homelab, through PROXY protocol (X-Real-Ip).
  • A private-only name returns 403 to the public.
  • A private-only subfolder of the root returns 403 to the public, and the rest of the root returns 200.
  • Passthrough of the wildcard.
  • The management API, which the node serves itself.
  • In cluster mode, the client address: the login page and the API on this node.
  • The health endpoint on port 80, which Bunny probes.
  • The redirect from HTTP to HTTPS.
  • A dedicated passthrough service, with the certificate of the origin.
  • A dedicated terminate service, with the certificate that HomeGAP orders for the nodes.
  • Raw TCP on the public port 19000.
  • The certificate on the node has no wildcard and no passthrough name. The ACME store of the node is empty.

The script also checks that the zone has the two CAA records.

items.title: The certificate of the nodes
items.text:
The pebble service is a local ACME server in place of Let's Encrypt. It accepts each challenge without a DNS lookup. Thus the harness checks that HomeGAP writes and removes the challenge records. It does not check that they resolve.

Pebble makes a new root certificate each time its container starts. run.sh reads the root and writes work/certs/trust.pem, which the viewer and the tunnels trust. After a new root, run.sh removes work/data/acme, so HomeGAP orders the certificate again.

items.title: Cluster checks
items.text:
e2e/config.e2e.yml has cluster mode on. With the cluster, run e2e/verify-cluster.sh after run.sh and verify.sh. It takes approximately 5 minutes, and most of that time is the switch-back hold.

e2e/verify-cluster.sh

The script has these sections:

  1. The database: every member is streaming, and the primary is on the homelab. The newest dump restores into an empty database.
  2. A user that the dashboard creates signs in at pangolin.<domain> through every node.
  3. A Pangolin client (the client service) reaches a private service through the node that it goes to. CLIENT_NODE_IP takes the role of DNS. Private-only names arrive from the private network.
  4. The homelab is cut off from the mesh. A node becomes the primary and takes writes, and the homelab stops writes. After the repair, HomeGAP switches the primary back.
  5. Exit nodes: a client that selects Exit via <node> or Exit via homelab reaches the internet through that exit. This section needs internet access.
  6. The container of Pangolin on each node cannot reach the etcd peer port or the Sentinel of a member. etcd and Sentinel refuse a request without their password.

To run only some sections, set ONLY, for example ONLY="3 5".

items.title: The homelab as a vote only
items.text:
To test cluster.homelab_role: vote, start a new harness with E2E_HOMELAB_ROLE=vote. The role does not change on a cluster that runs. Thus use a different project name and an empty e2e/work folder:

COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=homegap-e2e-vote E2E_HOMELAB_ROLE=vote E2E_NO_ENV=1 e2e/run.sh
COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=homegap-e2e-vote e2e/verify-cluster.sh

E2E_NO_ENV=1 makes run.sh ignore the .env file, so the harness does not activate a license key on the new database. In this mode, section 1 also checks that the database containers of the homelab are idle and that a dump is at home. Section 4 isolates the homelab from the mesh, then stops the database of the primary node.

Two harnesses cannot run at the same time, because they use the same addresses and ports. Before you start the second harness, run docker compose down in e2e/ for the first one.

Note

If you recreate a node container of the harness, recreate the gerbil, traefik and maintenance containers in it. Also recreate the connector in /opt/homegap/exit. The Docker daemon in the fake node gives its networks new subnets, and these containers keep the old ones. A reboot of a real server does not do this.

items.title: Writing style guide
items.text: This page is the brief for everyone who writes HomeGAP documentation, people and agents alike. The rules are a working profile of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE), adapted for software documentation, plus rules for accuracy and for a natural, human voice.

items.title: Part 0: Role and scope
items.text:
You write and edit the HomeGAP documentation in docs/. You get a brief for each page. The brief lists the facts, the sources in the code, and the order of the page.

  • Use only the facts in the brief, or facts you confirm in the source files that the brief names.
  • Do not add a feature, option, default, number, command, UI label, file path or behavior that the brief or the source does not show.
  • If a fact that you need is not in the brief, and you cannot confirm it in the source, do not guess. Put an HTML comment <!-- FACT-CHECK: what is missing --> at that location and list it in your report.
  • Write only files under docs/. Do not change code, mkdocs.yml or other files, unless the brief tells you to.
  • Use example.net for domains, na1, eu1, as1 for node ids and documentation addresses (203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24) for public IP addresses. Never use a real domain, a real person's name or a real location of a user's homelab.

items.title: Part 1: The nine grammatical and structural pillars
Section 1: Words and parts of speech
items.text:
• Rule 1.1: One word, one meaning. Use each word as one part of speech, with one meaning.
    • Use "close" only as a verb ("Close the dialog"). For the adjective, use "near".
    • Use "oil" only as a noun. Write "Apply oil to the bearing", not "Oil the bearing".
  • Rule 1.2: Use verbs for actions, not nouns made from verbs.
    • Not: "Perform an inspection of the seal." / "Execute the alignment."
    • Write: "Inspect the seal." / "Align the component."
  • Rule 1.3: Do not use phrasal verbs.
    • Not: "set up", "put together", "take apart", "carry out", "turn on", "find out".
    • Write: "prepare" or "configure", "assemble", "disassemble", "do", "enable" or "start", "learn" or "find".
    • Exception: a phrasal verb that is a name in a UI or a command (the Add node button, docker compose up) stays as it is.

items.title: Section 2: Noun clusters
items.text:
• Rule 2.1: Not more than three nouns in a row. Break longer clusters with prepositions.
    • Not: "node cluster member database container restart".
    • Write: "a restart of the database container on the node's cluster member".
    • Exception: a technical name stays as it is (cluster-proxy, "Pangolin EE license key").

items.title: Section 3: Verbs and tenses
items.text:
• Rule 3.1: Use only three verb forms.
    1. The infinitive, for a purpose: "To add a node, ...".
    2. The imperative, for a step: "Open", "Set", "Run".
    3. The present simple, for a description: "The orchestrator reads the labels."
  • Rule 3.2: No compound or future tenses. Use the past participle only as an adjective before a noun ("the saved stack"). Do not write "will", "has been", "will have".
    • Not: "The node will be removed from DNS."
    • Write: "HomeGAP removes the node from DNS."
  • Rule 3.3: Do not use "-ing" forms for actions or states.
    • Not: "While provisioning the node, ..." / "The tunnel is reconnecting."
    • Write: "During provisioning, ..." / "The tunnel reconnects."
    • Exception: a technical name or UI text with "-ing" stays as it is (provisioning…, "Pending switch-back", the streaming replica state, ping).

items.title: Section 4: Sentences
items.text:
• Rule 4.1: Word limits.
    • A procedural sentence (a step): 20 words or fewer.
    • A descriptive sentence: 25 words or fewer.
    • Code, labels, paths and URLs count as one word each.
  • Rule 4.2: One idea in each sentence. A sentence can have one dependent clause, if that clause gives a simple condition ("If the tunnel is down, ...").
  • Rule 4.3: No hedging. Do not use should, would, may, might, likely, probably, could, perhaps, usually (unless the code shows a real "usually", give the condition).
    • For a requirement, use must.
    • For a capability, use can.
    • For a recommendation, say it directly: "We recommend ...", or give the reason: "Use tunnels.mtu: 1420. The default of 1280 decreases throughput."

items.title: Section 5: Procedures
items.text:
