• Rule 5.1: One action in each step. Put each action in its own numbered step. A step can have a second sentence that tells the result ("The dashboard shows the node as provisioning….").
  • Rule 5.2: Condition before command. Give the condition, the requirement or the precaution before the action.
    • Not: "Press Run after you test the connection."
    • Write: "Test the connection. Then click Run." or "When the test passes, click Run."

items.title: Section 6: Descriptions
items.text: • Rule 6.1: Not more than six sentences in a paragraph. Do not put descriptive text and numbered steps in the same block. Put the description first, then the procedure.

items.title: Section 7: Safety messages
items.text:
• Rule 7.1: Mark each risk clearly, and isolate it. Start with the condition or the action, then give the risk.
    • Use !!! danger "Warning" when there is a risk of data loss, of lockout from a server, or of exposure of a private service or a secret.
    • Use !!! warning "Caution" when there is a risk of an interruption of service or of a failed operation.
    • Use !!! note for information that is not a risk, and !!! tip for a shortcut.
    • Example: "If you restrict SSH with ssh_allow_from and your public IP address changes, the orchestrator cannot connect to the node."

items.title: Sections 8 and 9: Punctuation and completeness
items.text:
• Rule 8.1: Do not drop words. Keep "the", "a" and "an". Keep verbs. No telegraphic text, also in table cells and list items that are sentences.
  • Rule 8.2: No semicolons. Make two sentences.

items.title: Part 2: Word list (one word, one meaning)
items.text:
Do not use Use begin, commence, initiate start utilize, employ, leverage use terminate, halt, conclude (as general verbs) stop or end perform, execute, carry out the specific verb (do, run, check, install) frequently, periodically the exact interval ("every 60 seconds") or often verify, ascertain, ensure make sure or check permit, allow (as general verbs) let, or say what a person can do set up configure or prepare (and the noun setup) take down stop or remove in order to to via through or with e.g., i.e. "for example", "that is"

Technical names (TN) and technical verbs. Keep words that are names of HomeGAP, Pangolin, Traefik, Bunny, Docker or Linux things, also if STE does not approve them. Examples: "orchestrator", "node", "front door", "passthrough", "terminate" (the TLS mode), "provision", "reconcile", "deploy", "label", "router", "middleware", "allowlist", "replica", "primary", "switchover", "failover", "connector", "tunnel", "blueprint". Write a name the same way every time.

Literal text is outside these rules. Code blocks, inline code, label names, config keys, commands, log lines, error messages and UI labels stay exactly as the source shows them. Quote a UI label in bold (Add node) and a value or key in code (homegap.tls).

items.title: Example 1: No passive voice, no hedging
items.text:
• Input: "It should be ensured that the interface cover is periodically checked by the maintenance crew to prevent any accumulating dust from causing a system malfunction."
  • STE: "The maintenance crew must check the interface cover every week. Dust can cause a system failure."
  • The passive "It should be ensured" and the hedge "should" are gone. The "-ing" form "accumulating" is gone. There are two short sentences, each with one idea.

items.title: Example 2: No noun clusters, no phrasal verbs
items.text:
• Input: "Before carrying out the automated backup system software configuration update, verify that the primary storage drive is completely empty."
  • STE: "Check the primary storage drive. Make sure that it is empty. Then, update the configuration of the software for the automated backup system."
  • The condition comes first. A preposition breaks the noun cluster. The phrasal verb "carrying out" is gone.

items.title: Example 3: HomeGAP text
items.text:
• Input: "Once you've set up the tunnels container, HomeGAP will automatically start routing your traffic through the nearest healthy node, which should give you seamless failover."
  • STE: "When the tunnels container runs, Bunny DNS sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. If a node fails its health check, Bunny removes it from the answers."

items.title: Part 4: A human voice
items.text:
STE limits the grammar. It does not make the text robotic. Write as an experienced engineer who explains the system to a colleague.

  • Be concrete. Give the real value, the real path and the real result. "The node returns a 503 page about 15 seconds after it loses the homelab" is better than "the system degrades gracefully".
  • Explain why, once. If a rule exists for a reason, give the reason in one sentence. Do not repeat it on the page.
  • Use "you" for the reader and the imperative for steps. Use "HomeGAP" or "the orchestrator" for the software, not "we", except in "We recommend".
  • Vary the sentence length inside the limits. Not every sentence has 20 words.
  • Use prose for explanations and lists for real lists (options, steps, items to check). A page that is only bullets is not acceptable.
  • Bold is for UI labels and for the first use of a defined term. Do not start each list item with a bold phrase. The exception is the feature list on the home page (and in the README), where each item starts with its point in bold.

items.title: Do not use these patterns
items.text:
They show that a text is generated, and they give no information:

  • Marketing words: seamless(ly), robust, powerful, effortless(ly), cutting-edge, game-changer, supercharge, unlock, elevate, streamline, empower, harness, delve, dive into, journey, landscape, realm, tapestry, crucial, vital, pivotal, essential (as filler), comprehensive, simply, just, easily, of course, it's worth noting, it's important to note, note that.
  • Openers and closers: "In this guide, ...", "Let's ...", "Whether you're ... or ...", "Welcome to ...", "In summary", "In conclusion", "That's it!", "Happy hosting!".
  • Rhetorical questions as headings or openers ("Why does this matter?").
  • Groups of three adjectives or three parallel phrases for rhythm only.
  • "Not only ... but also ...", "It's not X, it's Y".
  • Em dashes. Use a period, a comma, a colon or parentheses.
  • Emoji, exclamation marks.
  • A summary at the end of a page that repeats the page.
  • Headings with a colon and a slogan ("Failover: Peace of Mind").

items.title: Part 5: Page format (Zensical)
items.text:
• One # heading at the top: the page title, in sentence case. Then one or two sentences that tell what the page is for.
  • ## for sections, ### for subsections. Do not go deeper than ####.
  • Code blocks have a language: yaml, bash, text, json. Commands that a reader runs are in bash blocks, one command per line, without a $ prompt.
  • Admonitions: see Rule 7.1. Use ??? (a closed block) for long optional detail.
  • Use content tabs (=== "Standalone" / === "Cluster") when one step is different in the two modes.
  • Links between pages are relative paths to the .md file (../cluster/index.md#the-vote).
  • Tables for reference data (labels, config keys, ports, API routes). Each cell that is a sentence follows the rules above.
  • The hg_version variable (in double braces) gives the version of the docs. Pages go through Jinja: text that has double braces or a brace with a percent sign (for example Go templates) goes in a Jinja raw block.
  • A screenshot that the maintainer must add is an HTML comment on its own line: <!-- SCREENSHOT: docs/img/<page>/<nn>-<what>.png | what the image shows -->.

items.title: Part 6: Process for each page
items.text:
1. Isolate. Divide the brief into descriptions and procedures.
  2. Draft. Write the page in the order of the brief.
  3. Lint. Find and replace the forbidden words, passive voice, "-ing" forms, hedges, semicolons and the patterns in Part 4.
  4. Measure. Make each sentence fit the word limits. Make each paragraph six sentences or fewer.
  5. Check the facts. Compare each statement with the brief or the source. Remove each statement that you cannot connect to a fact.
  6. Report. After you write the files, report the files that you wrote, each FACT-CHECK comment and each fact in the brief that you think is wrong or unclear. Do not explain your edits.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: This page gives the full order of setup. Each step links to the page with the details.

items.title: The order of setup
items.text:
1. Read How HomeGAP works.
  2. Check the Requirements.
  3. Choose standalone or cluster mode.
  4. Prepare Bunny DNS: a zone and an API key.
  5. Prepare the servers: one VPS for each region.
  6. Install on the homelab: the compose file, the config and the secrets. Start in dry run.
  7. Add a node with the wizard on the dashboard, or by hand.
  8. Publish a service and check it.

In cluster mode, do two more steps. Add users on the Access page (Users and devices). Then connect the Pangolin apps.

items.title: What the orchestrator does after you start it
items.text:
You do the steps above one time. After that, the orchestrator does this work by itself:

  • In cluster mode, it prepares the private mesh and the shared database. The homelab member comes first, then each node.
  • It provisions each node: Docker, ufw, Pangolin, Gerbil and Traefik. It also installs the secrets and the certificate, and creates the admin account, the org and the API key. If you set a Pangolin EE license key, it activates the key.
  • It creates the homelab sites on the Pangolin of each node, and one Newt connector for each node.
  • It creates the Pangolin resources, and the Bunny geo records with their monitors.

items.title: Before production
items.text:
Do these checks on the test domain:

  • All nodes are green on the dashboard.
  • Each name resolves to the correct node in each region.
  • Failover works.
  • The change between passthrough and terminate works.

When all checks pass, set domain to your production domain. Then move that domain to Bunny DNS.

items.title: Add a node
items.text: The add-node wizard takes a fresh VPS from the initial login of your provider to a provisioned node. This page tells you how to use the wizard, and how to add a node by hand.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
The wizard writes the node to the config file. Thus dashboard.allow_config_edits must be true (the default), and the config mount of the orchestrator must be writable. Before each write, HomeGAP saves a backup of the file as <config>.bak-<millis>.

Setup runs on the orchestrator as a background job. You can leave the page while the job runs.

items.title: How setup protects your access
items.text:
Setup logs in one time with the initial credentials, and it does every step through that one connection. If the server has a login blocker (fail2ban, sshguard or CrowdSec), setup first exempts the address of the orchestrator, as the server sees it. It also removes any current ban on that address.

Setup proves each change before it keeps the change:

  • Before it hardens SSH, setup checks the key login and the passwordless sudo of the new user over a fresh connection.
  • Setup writes the SSH settings to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-homegap.conf, which comes before the drop-in file of cloud-init. It checks the syntax of the file.
  • Setup checks the effective SSH values with sshd -T -C for root, the login user and the management user, from the address of the orchestrator. Thus it finds a Match block that overrides the settings.
  • After the change, a fresh key login must work. If it does not work, setup restores the previous settings.
  • Before a change to the SSH settings or the firewall, setup arms a timer on the node. The timer reverts the change after two minutes. Setup disarms it only after a fresh login works.

If the orchestrator loses the connection to the node during a change, the node reverts the change by itself.

The password is for the setup job only. HomeGAP never writes it to disk or to the config. The password goes to ssh through SSH_ASKPASS, and to sudo on its standard input.

items.title: Open the wizard
items.text:
1. On the dashboard, open Nodes.
  2. Click Add node. The page shows "Set up a fresh server from its initial login and provision it".

items.title: 1. Server
items.text:
1. In Node id, type the id of the node, for example eu1. Use lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Start with a letter.
  2. In Public IP or host name, type the address of the server.
  3. In SSH port, type the SSH port. The default is 22.
  4. Set the location. Search the known data-center cities (for example "dallas", "london" or "hetzner"), or click a point in Pick on the map.
  5. Optional: correct Region code, Latitude, Longitude or Place name.
  6. Optional: type the Provider.
  7. Click Continue.

When you pick a point on the map, the nearest known city within 50 km gives the point its name.

items.title: 2. Initial login
items.text:
1. In User, type root or another user that can use sudo.
  2. Select Password or Private key.
  3. For Password, type the password.
  4. For Private key, type the path of the key file in Private key on the orchestrator.
  5. Click Test connection.
  6. For a password login to a new server, the page shows "Check the server's fingerprint". Compare the Host key fingerprint with the fingerprint in the console of your provider.
  7. If the fingerprints are the same, click The fingerprint matches. HomeGAP then sends the password and does the test.
  8. Click Continue.

HomeGAP sends a password only to a host key that you confirmed. A server that shows a different key later does not get the password.

You must test the connection before you can continue. The test checks the login and shows this information:

  • The OS, as Connected to <os> <version> (<arch>).
  • Root access: how the user gets root access.
  • Docker: if Docker is installed.
  • Host key: the fingerprint of the host key of the server.
  • Orchestrator seen from: the address of the orchestrator, as the node sees it.

If the host key is different from the last connection, the test reports it. Make sure that the server has a new install. Then click Forget the old host key and retry.

items.title: 3. Access
items.text:
The Management user is "The account HomeGAP manages the node with."

  1. Keep Create a dedicated user selected. The default User name is homegap. This user has passwordless sudo and logs in over SSH with a key only.
  2. Optional: select Add it to the docker group.
  3. Under SSH key, select Generate a new key, Paste a private key or Use a key file on the orchestrator.
  4. Click Generate key or Use this key. The page shows "Key ready" and the fingerprint.
  5. Optional: under SSH hardening, select Disable root login. This option needs a management user other than root.
  6. Optional: select Disable password login. Then SSH accepts keys only, for every user.
  7. Click Continue.

A generated key is an ed25519 key. HomeGAP keeps it in <data dir>/ssh/ on the orchestrator.

HomeGAP uses sudo only for system changes: packages, the firewall, WireGuard and sysctls. The files under the install directory (/opt/homegap by default) belong to the management user. If the user is in the docker group, HomeGAP also runs Docker Compose as this user, so docker compose works there without sudo. The data directories of the cluster member stay with their containers.

items.title: 4. Firewall
items.text:
1. Keep Let HomeGAP manage the firewall selected. HomeGAP keeps the rules in sync on each provisioning pass.
  2. Under SSH from, select Anywhere or Only these sources.
  3. For Only these sources, check the list in Allowed sources. The wizard fills it with the address from the connection test.
  4. Click Continue.

The page shows the rules:

  • SSH on its port (tcp), from anywhere or from the sources in the list.
  • HTTP 80/tcp, HTTPS 443/tcp and 443/udp.
  • WireGuard 51820/udp and 21820/udp.
  • The ports of raw TCP and UDP services, as their labels set them.

Warning

This risk applies to Only these sources. If the public IP address of the orchestrator changes to an address outside the list, HomeGAP loses SSH access to the node. This occurs with a residential IP address, a new ISP or a homelab in a new location. Provisioning and health checks for that node then fail until you correct the rule.

Use a stable address range. Or open SSH to anywhere and disable password login.

To recover, log in through the web console of your provider. Run ufw allow <ssh port>/tcp. Then update ssh_allow_from in the config. The next pass replaces the rules.

items.title: 5. Review & run
items.text:
1. Examine the summary.
  2. Click Set up and add node. The page shows the progress of each setup step.
  3. When the page shows "Done. Provisioning starts on the next reconcile pass.", click Go to nodes.

items.title: If setup fails
items.text:
A failed job shows the step with the failure and the reason. Correct the cause, then click Retry.

You can run setup again safely. The completed steps are idempotent. If an earlier run already disabled password login, setup continues with the key of the node.

items.title: After the wizard
items.text:
Provisioning runs in the background. The first install takes a few minutes for Docker, the firewall and the Pangolin stack. During this time, the node shows provisioning… on the Nodes page.

If the first provisioning fails, HomeGAP tries again after five minutes. To try again at once, click Re-provision.

items.title: Add a node by hand
items.text: You can also prepare the server yourself and add the node to nodes[] in the config. See the "By hand" tab in Prepare the servers.

items.title: Prepare Bunny DNS
items.text: HomeGAP uses Bunny DNS to send each viewer to the nearest healthy node. This page tells you how to prepare the DNS zone and the API key.

items.title: What HomeGAP needs
items.text:
HomeGAP needs two things from Bunny:

  • A DNS zone that is equal to domain or a parent of it. The config key is bunny.zone. Validation fails if the zone is not equal to domain or a parent of it.
  • The API key of your Bunny account. The orchestrator reads it from an environment variable (default name BUNNY_API_KEY, config key bunny.api_key_env) or from a file (bunny.api_key_file).

HomeGAP sends the key in the AccessKey header to https://api.bunny.net. It finds the zone by its name and creates all the records itself. You do not create records.

items.title: Prepare the zone and the key
items.text:
1. Choose a test domain. Use a spare domain, or a subdomain of your real domain, for example gap.example.net.
  2. Sign in to Bunny (bunny.net). Open the DNS section https://dash.bunny.net/dns/zones
  3. Add a DNS zone for the domain or the subdomain.
  4. Point the domain at the nameservers of Bunny. Do the step that matches your domain:
    • For a whole domain, go to your registrar. Replace the nameservers with the nameservers that Bunny shows for the zone.
    • For a subdomain, go to the current DNS provider of the parent zone. Add NS records for the subdomain there.
  5. Wait until Bunny shows the zone as active. To check the delegation, run this command: 
    dig NS gap.example.net +short
    The command shows the nameservers of Bunny.
  6. Copy the API key of your account from the Bunny account settings: https://dash.bunny.net/account/api-key
  7. Keep the key for the install. You put it in .env as BUNNY_API_KEY. See Install on the homelab.

items.title: Records at the names that HomeGAP manages
items.text:
Warning

On each pass that is not a dry run, HomeGAP deletes records that collide with its managed record sets. This occurs at each name that HomeGAP manages: the root, *.<domain>, the dedicated hostnames, the node management hosts and the other managed names.

  • HomeGAP deletes an A or AAAA record that it did not create, if it has the same name and type as a managed record.
  • HomeGAP deletes any CNAME record at a managed name.
  • HomeGAP adopts an unmanaged record that has exactly the desired value.

Before you disable dry run, open the Config page on the dashboard. Find the delete rows in the diff, and write down the records that you want to keep.

HomeGAP never touches records at other names. It marks its own records with the comment managed-by:homegap <purpose> node=<id>.

items.title: What HomeGAP creates
items.text:
Name Record When <domain> A geo record set (the front door). When a front door exists. *.<domain> A geo record set (the front door). When the front door has homegap.wildcard: "true". A public dedicated hostname A geo record set. For each public service with its own hostname. pangolin-<node>.<domain> A plain record (the management host of the node). For each node. pangolin.<domain> A geo record set. In cluster mode. speedtest.<domain> A geo record set for the speed test. With the speed test, and only if there is no wildcard. speedtest-<node>.<domain> A record for each node. With the speed test. status.<domain> A geo record set. With the status page. status-<node>.<domain> A record for each node. With the status page.

HomeGAP creates A records, and AAAA records for nodes with public_ipv6. The TTL comes from bunny.ttl (default 60). The monitor comes from bunny.monitor (default http). Only geo records get a monitor.

For the routing and the monitors, see DNS routing and health checks.

items.title: Standalone or cluster
items.text:
HomeGAP has two modes. This page helps you choose one before you deploy.

Caution

Choose the mode when you deploy. HomeGAP does not support the addition or removal of cluster: on a deployment that runs. A node that HomeGAP provisions in one mode keeps the stack of that mode until you remove the node and add it again.

items.title: Standalone mode
items.text:
In standalone mode, the config has no cluster: key. Each node runs its own Pangolin with its own SQLite database.

Private services and users are different on each node. If you need EE features, each node needs its own EE license key, because a key binds to one Pangolin instance. Standalone mode is simpler and has fewer containers.

items.title: Cluster mode
items.text:
In cluster mode, the config has a cluster: key. All nodes are one Pangolin EE cluster with one org, one set of users and one license.

The cluster uses a shared database with a member on the homelab and on every node. The database uses PostgreSQL under Patroni, Valkey with Sentinel, etcd for the vote and HAProxy. The members connect over a private WireGuard mesh, hg-mesh.

The Pangolin apps connect to pangolin.<domain>. Bunny DNS sends this name to the nearest healthy node. Thus the apps continue to work while the homelab is down, and sign-in also works. You manage users and devices on the Access page, and you can offer exit nodes.

The cluster uses the PostgreSQL build of Pangolin. The image tag ee-<version> becomes ee-postgresql-<version>.

We recommend cluster mode with two or more nodes. The vote needs a majority. With the homelab and only one node, the loss of either one stops all writes to the database.

items.title: Comparison
items.text: Standalone Cluster Pangolin instances One independent Pangolin on each node. One Pangolin EE cluster on all nodes. Users and sign-in A different set on each node. One set of users for all nodes. EE license keys One key for each node. One key for the cluster. Homelab down Public homelab services are down. The Pangolin of each node keeps its own state. Public homelab services are down. The apps stay connected. New sign-ins work approximately 30 seconds later, when the nodes elect a primary. Extra containers None. Each node runs five: etcd, PostgreSQL with Patroni, Valkey, Valkey Sentinel and HAProxy. The nodes also run a mesh probe. The homelab member runs four: etcd, PostgreSQL with Patroni, Valkey and Valkey Sentinel (no HAProxy). Exit nodes Not available. Available. Access page Not available. Available.

items.title: Enable cluster mode
items.text:
To use all the defaults, add this line to the config file:

cluster: {}

For the options, see the Configuration reference. For the full description of the cluster, see Cluster mode.

items.title: Publish a service
items.text: This page tells you how to send the first real traffic through HomeGAP, and how to check the result.

items.title: Publish through the front door
items.text:
The front door claims the root domain and *.<domain>. Thus HomeGAP publishes each name that your homelab Traefik serves under the domain, and you add no more labels.

To publish a service, add a normal Traefik router at home, for example with the rule Host(`whoami.example.net`).

A service that needs its own path gets its own homegap.* labels. This applies to a dedicated hostname, a raw TCP or UDP service and a private service. See the Label reference. A Docker event starts a pass at once, so the change starts without a wait for the next resync.

items.title: Check the service
items.text:
Run these commands from any network:

dig +short example.net
dig +short whoami.example.net
curl -sv https://whoami.example.net/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'subject:|HTTP/'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://203.0.113.10/

The results are as follows:

  • The two dig commands return node addresses. The wildcard record covers whoami.
  • The curl command to https:// shows the certificate of your homelab. In passthrough mode, the homelab Traefik ends TLS.
  • The curl command to http://<node ip>/ sends the same request as the Bunny monitor. The request goes through the tunnel to the health check path of the front door. It returns 502 when the origin is down.

On the dashboard, the Overview and Services pages show the health in each region. The DNS page shows the records and the state of their monitors.

Note

One node gives no failover. With a single record for each name, Bunny continues to answer with that node when it is down. For failover, you need a second node.

items.title: Label errors
items.text:
The dashboard and the log show label errors for each container. An error in the labels of one container never stops the other services. These are examples of errors:

  • An unknown protocol.
  • Pangolin sign-in (homegap.auth) without homegap.tls: terminate.
  • A reserved public port.
  • A hostname that two services claim.

An unknown homegap.* label gives a warning, and HomeGAP ignores it.

items.title: How HomeGAP works
items.text: This page gives the model of the system: the parts, the path of a request, the reconcile loop and failover. Later pages give the details.

items.title: The parts
items.text:
Part What runs there Homelab Docker, the homelab Traefik (the front door), your services, the orchestrator (homegap run) and the tunnel supervisor (homegap tunnels, the tunnels container). In cluster mode, also a cluster member with PostgreSQL, Valkey and etcd. Nodes Pangolin, Gerbil (WireGuard) and Traefik. In cluster mode, also a cluster member. Bunny DNS The DNS zone for your domain, with geo routing and health monitors.

The homelab has no inbound ports. All connections between the homelab and the nodes start at the homelab.

items.title: The path of a request
items.text:
This is the default path: the front door in passthrough mode.

  1. A viewer resolves a name. Bunny DNS answers with the nearest healthy node.
  2. The viewer connects to that node on port 443.
  3. A Traefik TCP router on the node reads the TLS SNI. It matches the root domain or any single label under the domain.
  4. The router forwards the stream, still encrypted, into a Pangolin TCP resource.
  5. The stream goes through the WireGuard tunnel to the homelab Traefik. The Newt connector for that node opens this tunnel outbound from home.
  6. The homelab Traefik ends TLS and routes the request to the service.

The node never sees plaintext. Authelia and the other parts of your homelab continue to work without changes. For the other paths, see Traffic paths.

The orchestrator is the control plane. It reads the Docker labels and writes the connector specs for the tunnel supervisor. It talks to the nodes over SSH and through the Pangolin API, and to Bunny through the Bunny API. It never carries traffic.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.text:
The orchestrator is a reconciler. It moves the actual state toward the desired state. The desired state is the Docker labels and the config file, and nothing else.

The work has six independent domains. A failure in one domain never stops the others.

Domain What it does Discovery Reads the homegap.* labels from Docker, through a proxy that accepts only read requests. If discovery fails, the orchestrator skips the Resources and DNS domains for that pass. An empty view can never delete anything. Nodes Uses SSH to change a bare Ubuntu VPS into a Pangolin node. The steps are preflight, Docker, ufw, the compose stack, the secrets, a health wait, the bootstrap and a final check. Tunnels Keeps a Pangolin site for the homelab on each node. Writes one Newt connector spec for each node, for the tunnel supervisor. The spec has the addresses of the node's management host, the same values as its DNS records. The supervisor pins them in the hosts file of the tunnels container, so a connector does not depend on public DNS. Resources Creates the Pangolin resources through blueprints, one for each resource, with fixed hg-* niceIds. Writes the Traefik routes of each node: SNI passthrough, health and the management API. DNS Keeps the Bunny geo record sets for the root, the wildcard and each dedicated hostname. Also keeps a plain record for the management host of each node. Asks the nameservers of the zone directly if they serve each plain record. Observability Collects the health of nodes, tunnels, resources and DNS for the dashboard.

In the Nodes domain, the bootstrap is headless. It creates the admin, the org, an API key with the least privilege and the license. Each step is idempotent. A drift check at an interval repairs changes from outside HomeGAP.

In the Resources domain, the orchestrator deletes only stale hg-* resources. It never touches a resource that it does not manage. Traefik on the node reloads the routes without a restart.

A pass is one run of the reconcile loop. Passes start in three ways:

  • On Docker events, after a debounce (default 2s).
  • At an interval, as a full resync (default every 60s).
  • On demand, with Resync on the dashboard.

Each pass applies only the minimum difference.

items.title: Health and failover
items.text:
Each geo record has a Bunny HTTP monitor. Bunny sends a request to http://<node-ip>/ every 30 seconds from three regions. On the node, this request goes through the tunnel to the health check path of the front door (homegap.healthcheck). Thus a node is healthy only when the node is up, its tunnel is up and the origin answers.

  • If the origin is down, the probe gets a 502.
  • If the tunnel is down, the probe fails within 5 seconds.

Bunny removes the offline members from a record set. Viewers then resolve to the next-nearest node. When all members are offline, Bunny returns all of them (fail-open).

A real failover takes the health interval, plus the 60-second TTL, plus the time that resolvers cache the answer. This is approximately 1 to 5 minutes.

When the homelab is down, the nodes show a "back shortly" page for passthrough sites. The page has HTTP status 503 and starts approximately 15 seconds after the nodes lose the homelab. Raw ports and resources that the node terminates fail.

For the monitors and the routing options, see DNS routing and health checks.

items.title: Standalone and cluster
items.text:
Without the cluster: key, each node runs an independent Pangolin. With cluster:, the Pangolin of each node is one instance of a single Pangolin EE cluster. The cluster has a shared database with a member on the homelab and on every node.

The members connect over a private WireGuard mesh. The homelab holds the database primary while it is up. While it is down, the nodes elect one of themselves. To compare the two modes, see Standalone or cluster.

items.title: Install on the homelab
items.text: This page tells you how to run the orchestrator and the tunnel supervisor with deploy/homelab-compose.yml. The first start is a dry run, so that you can examine the changes before HomeGAP makes them.

items.title: The image
items.text: The image is ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The same image runs the orchestrator (homegap run) and the tunnel supervisor (homegap tunnels).

items.title: The folder
items.text:
Put these files in one folder:

Path Content compose.yml A copy of deploy/homelab-compose.yml. config/config.yml The config file. secrets/ssh/<node id> The private SSH keys, if you add nodes by hand. .env The secrets. Use mode 600, and never commit this file. backups/ In cluster mode, the nightly pg_dump files. HomeGAP keeps the newest seven.

items.title: The compose services
items.text: Service What it does homegap-mesh A busybox container that holds the network namespace of the cluster. The mesh interface (hg-mesh) and the cluster containers of the homelab are in it. homegap-mesh-agent The same image as the orchestrator, with the command mesh. It keeps the mesh interface and the firewall of that namespace. HomeGAP uses it only with cluster:. orchestrator The image ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap:latest with the command run. It drops all capabilities except NET_ADMIN and DAC_OVERRIDE. docker-proxy A filter in front of the Docker socket. The orchestrator reads the container list, the events and the image data through it. homegap-etcd, homegap-db, homegap-valkey, homegap-sentinel The cluster member of the homelab. HomeGAP uses them only with cluster:. tunnels The same image with the command tunnels --dir /tunnels. It keeps one Newt connector for each node.

items.title: homegap-mesh
items.text:
The service holds a network namespace for the cluster only. The orchestrator is not in it. It is on one network, homegap-cluster, which it shares with the orchestrator. See Cluster mesh.

The service uses a fixed image. Do not recreate it when you update HomeGAP. A new container replaces the namespace and drops the mesh.

items.title: homegap-mesh-agent
items.text: The agent is the only container in the namespace of homegap-mesh that can change the network. It has NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW. It shares the homegap-mesh volume with the orchestrator. Without cluster:, it waits.

items.title: orchestrator
items.text:
Put the published ports and the Traefik labels of the dashboard on this service. It is on three networks: traefik, homegap-docker (where it reaches docker-proxy) and homegap-cluster (where it reaches the cluster).

The orchestrator reads these environment variables:

  • BUNNY_API_KEY. It is necessary.
  • PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY. It is optional.
  • HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN. The bearer token of the dashboard. If it is empty, HomeGAP creates a token.
  • DOCKER_HOST. The address of docker-proxy.
  • HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN. It is optional.

The orchestrator has these volumes:

  • ./config/config.yml:/config/config.yml. This mount must be writable only if you enable config edits on the dashboard.
  • ./secrets/ssh:/secrets/ssh:ro. The SSH keys of the nodes.
  • homegap-data:/data. The state cache, known_hosts, the generated SSH keys and the dashboard token. No other container mounts this volume.
  • homegap-cluster-config:/cluster-config. The config that the orchestrator writes for the cluster containers. They mount it read-only at /config.
  • homegap-tunnels:/tunnels. The connector specs. The tunnels container mounts the same volume at /tunnels.
  • homegap-mesh:/mesh. The description of the mesh. The mesh agent mounts the same volume at /mesh.

The paths /cluster-config, /tunnels and /mesh are fixed in the HomeGAP image. You set no variable for them. Mount each volume at its path in both containers that share it.

If a shared directory is not a volume, the other container cannot see it. Then the orchestrator writes an error with the path and the name of the volume to its log at start.

The orchestrator does not mount the Docker socket. See Security model.

items.title: docker-proxy
items.text: The service mounts the Docker socket and accepts only GET requests for containers, images and events. It is only on the homegap-docker network, so no other container can reach it.

items.title: The cluster member
items.text:
Without cluster mode, you can remove homegap-etcd, homegap-db, homegap-valkey and homegap-sentinel. In cluster mode, they wait until the orchestrator writes their config to the homegap-cluster-config volume. While they wait, their log shows "waiting for ... (written by the HomeGAP orchestrator)".

The file limits the log of each service to 30 MB (x-logging).

items.title: tunnels
items.text:
The tunnel supervisor is independent of the orchestrator. If the orchestrator stops, the tunnels stay up. It shares only the homegap-tunnels volume with the orchestrator.

The tunnels service must share a Docker network with Traefik. It must also share a network with each service that HomeGAP exposes directly, that is raw TCP and UDP services and dedicated subdomains.

For tunnels.native: true, the service needs cap_add: [NET_ADMIN] and devices: ["/dev/net/tun:/dev/net/tun"].

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Copy deploy/homelab-compose.yml to compose.yml in your folder.
  2. Copy config/config.example.yml to config/config.yml.
  3. In config/config.yml, set domain, bunny.zone and pangolin.acme_email.
  4. Read Certificates. HomeGAP publishes CAA records for your domain, and they also apply to the Traefik of your homelab.
  5. Add the nodes to nodes[]. To use the wizard, set nodes: [] instead. The wizard writes each node to the config file.
  6. For cluster mode, add cluster: {}.
  7. For the first start, set reconcile.dry_run: true.
  8. Create .env next to compose.yml, with this content: 
    BUNNY_API_KEY=...
PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY=...
HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN=...
    PANGOLIN_LICENSE_KEY is optional. For HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN, use a long random string.
  9. Make sure that the config has dashboard.auth_token_env: HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN. The example config has it.
  10. If you set no dashboard token, read the token that HomeGAP creates after the first start. See Dashboard.
  11. Make the file readable only by you: 
    chmod 600 .env
  12. Make sure that your Traefik network exists. Its name must match the external network networks.traefik in compose.yml.
  13. Add the front door labels to your homelab Traefik container: 
    labels:
  homegap.expose: "example.net"
  homegap.wildcard: "true"
  homegap.protocol: "https"
  homegap.tls: "passthrough"
    If the HTTPS entrypoint of Traefik does not listen on 443 inside its container, also add homegap.port: "<that port>".
  14. Add the HTTP provider of HomeGAP to the static configuration of your homelab Traefik. With it, Traefik answers 421 for the names that only the nodes serve. See When a browser uses one connection for two names. 
    providers:
  http:
    endpoint: http://orchestrator:8088/api/traefik/homelab
    pollInterval: 30s
    Keep your other providers. Traefik can use the file provider and the HTTP provider at the same time. The address is the dashboard of the orchestrator, on the traefik network. The dashboard must listen on that network: dashboard.bind: 0.0.0.0:8088, as in the example config. Traefik does not need the dashboard token for this address. The orchestrator accepts a request from the front door container that Traefik did not forward for another client.
  15. Recreate the Traefik container, so that it gets the labels and the provider.
  16. Start the services: 
    docker compose up -d
  17. Look at the log of the orchestrator: 
    docker compose logs -f orchestrator
  18. Check the config: 
    docker compose exec orchestrator homegap validate
    The command prints OK: N node(s), domain ..., zone ..., or the list of errors.

items.title: Open the dashboard
items.text:
Warning

Never expose the dashboard publicly. The dashboard has control of every node.

For a first look, publish the dashboard only on the loopback address of the homelab. Then use an SSH tunnel from your workstation.

  1. On the orchestrator service, add ports: ["127.0.0.1:8088:8088"].
  2. Recreate the service: 
    docker compose up -d
  3. On your workstation, open the SSH tunnel: 
    ssh -L 8088:127.0.0.1:8088 <homelab>
  4. Open http://localhost:8088 in your browser. If you set a token, the dashboard asks for it.

For the long term, publish the dashboard as a private Pangolin resource. See Private services.

items.title: Disable dry run
items.text:
In dry run, the orchestrator does full discovery and writes the desired state to the log. It makes no SSH, API or DNS writes.

  1. Open the Config page on the dashboard.
  2. Examine the diff between the desired state and the actual state.
  3. Make sure that each secret in the config shows as present. The page never shows the values.
  4. Set reconcile.dry_run: false in config/config.yml. The orchestrator reads the file again on each pass, so you do not restart it.

If you use HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN instead, remove it from the environment of the orchestrator service. Then run docker compose up -d to recreate the container.

items.title: Dry run reference
items.text:
Each of these starts the orchestrator in dry run:

  • The environment variable HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN with the value true, 1 or yes.
  • The option --dry-run of homegap run.
  • The config key reconcile.dry_run: true.

To see what a set of labels produces without Docker, use homegap plan:

homegap plan --labels labels.json

The file labels.json is a JSON map of container names to labels.

If you make an edit to the config that is not valid, the orchestrator writes the error to the log. The last good config stays in effect.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
This page lists what you must have before you install HomeGAP.

Component Requirement Homelab Docker with Compose, and a Traefik instance in front of your services. Regional nodes A VPS with Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 or 26.10 (x86_64 or aarch64), a public IPv4 address (IPv6 is optional) and SSH access. DNS A Bunny DNS zone and a Bunny API key. Pangolin EE license Only for cluster mode and for wildcard resources in terminate mode. Use one key for a cluster, or one key for each node without a cluster. See Pangolin EE licenses. Nodes for the cluster Two or more. Then the cluster can elect a primary, and sign-in continues to work, while the homelab is down.

items.title: The homelab
items.text:
The homelab compose file expects the Docker network of your Traefik as an external network with the name traefik. If your network has a different name, change the name in the compose file.

Cluster mode needs WireGuard in the kernel of the homelab host, for the mesh interface hg-mesh. The setting tunnels.native: true also needs it. WireGuard is part of Linux 5.6 and later.

items.title: SSH access to the nodes
items.text:
HomeGAP accepts two types of SSH access:

  • Root, or a user with sudo, with a password or a key. The add-node wizard prepares the rest. See Add a node.
  • A user with passwordless sudo and a key that you configure yourself. See Prepare the servers.

items.title: Network access
items.text:
The orchestrator needs outbound access to these destinations:

  • The nodes, over SSH.
  • The Bunny API at api.bunny.net. The config key bunny.api_url sets the URL (default https://api.bunny.net).
  • The container registries.

The orchestrator needs no inbound access.

items.title: Prepare the servers
items.text: This page tells you what to create at your VPS provider. It also gives the two ways to give HomeGAP access to the servers.

items.title: Create the servers
items.text:
Create one VPS for each region. You can use any provider. Each server must have:

  • Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 or 26.10.
  • An x86_64 or aarch64 CPU.
  • A public IPv4 address. IPv6 is optional.

Write down the public IP address, the SSH port and the initial login that the provider gives you. The initial login is a root password or a key.

items.title: The firewall on the node
items.text:
By default, HomeGAP manages ufw on each node (nodes[].firewall, default true). The firewall opens only these ports:

  • SSH, from anywhere or only from the sources in ssh_allow_from.
  • 80/tcp, 443/tcp and 443/udp.
  • 51820/udp and 21820/udp, for WireGuard and Gerbil.
  • In cluster mode, cluster.mesh.port/udp (default 51821).
  • The public ports of raw TCP and UDP services, as their labels set them.

A firewall at the provider level (for example a security group) is outside the control of HomeGAP. It must also open the same ports.

HomeGAP installs Docker on the node if Docker is not there (install_docker, default true).

items.title: Give HomeGAP access
items.text:
With the wizard (recommended)By hand

Keep the initial root login from your provider, with its password or its key. You do not prepare anything else on the server.

When the orchestrator runs, continue at Add a node. The wizard uses the initial login to create the management user and the SSH key.

Create a user with passwordless sudo and a dedicated SSH key for each node. Then add the node to nodes[] in the config.

Run these commands on the homelab, in the HomeGAP folder. Replace the user, the address and the node id with your values.

  1. Create the folder for the keys: 
    mkdir -p secrets/ssh
  2. Create a key for the node: 
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C homegap-na1 -f secrets/ssh/na1
  3. Make the private key readable only by you: 
    chmod 600 secrets/ssh/na1
  4. Copy the public key to the server: 
    ssh-copy-id -i secrets/ssh/na1.pub deploy@203.0.113.10
  5. Give the user passwordless sudo: 
    ssh -t -i secrets/ssh/na1 deploy@203.0.113.10 'echo "deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/homegap >/dev/null && sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/homegap'
  6. Test the login and sudo: 
    ssh -i secrets/ssh/na1 -o BatchMode=yes deploy@203.0.113.10 'sudo -n true && echo ok'
    The command must print ok without a prompt.
  7. Add the node to nodes[] in config/config.yml: 
    nodes:
  - id: na1
    region: NA
    host: 203.0.113.10
    ssh_user: deploy
    ssh_key_file: /secrets/ssh/na1
    location: { latitude: 40.71, longitude: -74.01, name: "New York" }

The ssh_key_file path is the path inside the orchestrator container. The compose file mounts ./secrets/ssh at /secrets/ssh.

These rules apply to the entry:

  • The node id must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$. It has lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and it starts with a letter.
  • If host is not an IPv4 address, set public_ipv4.
  • With bunny.routing: geolocation (the default), each node needs a location or a known region code. The codes are NA, SA, EU, AF, ME, AS and OC.

For all the node keys, see the Configuration reference.

items.title: The dashboard
items.text:
The orchestrator serves a dashboard on dashboard.bind. This page tells you how to reach it safely and what each page shows.

Warning

If the dashboard is public, anybody can control every node. Reach it only through a private Pangolin resource or an SSH tunnel. See Private services.

items.title: Access
items.text:
A bearer token protects every /api route. Set it with dashboard.auth_token_env or dashboard.auth_token_file. If the config names no token, or the token is not available, HomeGAP creates one. It keeps that token in the file dashboard-token in its data directory, with mode 0600. To read the token, run this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator cat /data/dashboard-token

The dashboard asks for the token in a sign-in dialog and keeps it in the browser. A change of the token needs a restart of the orchestrator.

To remove the token from the browser, click Sign out at the bottom of the menu, or search for "Sign out". Do this on a computer that other people use.

The dashboard updates live. It uses one server-sent event stream (/api/events). After the first snapshot, the stream sends only the parts that change. When the browser tab is hidden for 30 seconds, the dashboard closes the stream. It opens the stream again when you return to the tab.

The orchestrator writes to the stream every 25 seconds or less. If the dashboard gets nothing for 60 seconds, it opens a new stream. The orchestrator keeps 32 streams open at most. A dashboard above that number gets an error until a different one closes.

If the dashboard cannot reach the orchestrator for more than 5 seconds, a dialog says so. The dialog shows the error and the time to the next try, and it has Reconnect now. It closes by itself when the orchestrator answers again. Until then, the page shows the last data from the orchestrator.

items.title: The layout
items.text:
The menu has two groups: Operate (Overview, Nodes, Services, Access, Speed test) and Plumbing (DNS, Tunnels, Activity, Diagnostics, Config). A number next to a page is the count of items that need attention there. On a tablet the menu is a rail of icons. On a phone it is a grid of icons under the header, which gets smaller when you scroll.

The box at the bottom of the menu shows the last pass, and two controls:

  • Resync queues a pass now.
  • Pause stops all changes everywhere. HomeGAP then only observes, and every page shows a banner with Resume. While changes are paused, the box offers Run one pass: one pass that applies changes, after which HomeGAP is paused again. A re-provision or a switch of the primary while paused asks if you want to apply just that change or resume everything.

Each page starts with a headline that states the answer, for example "5 of 6 edges healthy.". Under it, a status line shows the most important message. When there are more, +N more opens all of them.

Select a node, a service or another item to open it in the Inspector. On a wide screen the Inspector is a column on the right. On a narrower screen it is a drawer, and on a phone it is a sheet at the bottom. The Inspector holds the actions for the item. Esc, the close button or the back button closes it. On a phone you can also drag the sheet down.

Press ⌘K, Ctrl+K or / to search everything: nodes, services, DNS records, tunnels, pages, actions such as Resync now, and on the orchestrator the log, the config keys and the secrets. The search shows the names of config keys and secrets, never their values.

Actions that are risky ask first. To remove a node or a person, you type its name. After you remove a node or a person, a message with Undo shows for 30 seconds. A later message does not replace it. Dismiss removes it. A removed person stays until then, and Undo keeps them. Undo on a removed node adds it back with its config.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The whole system at a glance:

  • The gauges: edges, tunnels, services, DNS, and in cluster mode the mesh links and the replica lag.
  • Needs attention: what is wrong now, worst first. Select an item to inspect it.
  • The network: the traffic path (homelab, tunnels, edges, names) or the map. The page remembers your choice. See Maps and locations.
  • Each edge's Pangolin API probe over the last hour.
  • Each service through each edge, in milliseconds.
  • The system and the recent changes.

items.title: Nodes
items.text:
The fleet table shows each node's health, its checks, its Pangolin API probe over the last hour, its tunnel, its certificate, its stack and its drift. While a stack update runs or is held, a strip above the table shows each node's part in the rollout.

Select a node to open it in the Inspector. The Inspector shows its graphs (the Pangolin API probe, the requests and the egress through its proxy, the mesh round trip and the tunnel), its checks, its system facts, its stack and its last 10 provisioning runs. While a job runs, the stack column shows its step, for example "writing the stack (4 of 7)". The actions on a node are Re-provision, Pause or Resume, Diagnostics, Speed test, Change location and Remove. Change location moves the node to a known city or a point on the map. Geo DNS and the maps use the new place from the next pass. After a removal, the action is Decommission. During a held rollout, the node also has Retry update and Skip update. See Manage nodes and Node updates and rollback.

+ Add node opens the wizard over the page. When a run fails, Retry runs each step again and keeps the user that the failed run made. If something blocked the new SSH connections of the orchestrator, the button shows a time, for example "Retry in 2:59". A retry before that time fails for the same reason. See Add a node. In cluster mode, the page also has the Cluster database and Cluster mesh panels. See Cluster mesh and Cluster database.

items.title: Services
items.text:
Each service, with its response time through each edge. Amber is slow (over 1 s). Rose is failing, with the status code. A dash means that the edge does not serve it. The orchestrator measures this on each pass with one request through each edge's proxy.

Filter by text, or show only the problems. Select a service to see how each edge serves it, how it is published and its source labels. Each service has Open, Pause or Resume, and Logs.

items.title: DNS
items.text: The records that HomeGAP manages, grouped into record sets. The page shows the state of each member, its monitor, and if it matches the desired state. A plain record is in sync only when each nameserver of the zone serves it. Geo record sets give a different answer in each location, so HomeGAP does not compare them. The geo steering strip shows which edges answer now and which are withdrawn, and for how long. The Inspector shows when HomeGAP last changed each record.

items.title: Tunnels
items.text: One card for each Newt connector: its state, its process, its restarts and its throughput over the last hour. The Inspector shows the Newt version and the last times the connector stopped, with the reason. Restart connector stops Newt and starts it again. Traffic through that node pauses for a few seconds.

items.title: Access
items.text: Who can sign in to the Pangolin apps, their invitations and their devices. The app address has a QR code for phones. Select a person to change their roles, then Save. An open invitation has New link, which makes a new invite link and stops the old one, and Revoke. Select a device to see when it was last seen. This page is available only in cluster mode. See Users and devices.

items.title: Speed test
items.text: Latency and throughput through the real traffic path. Test all nodes tests each node in turn on the orchestrator, so the run continues when you close the page. The gauge is white for ping, cyan for download and violet for upload. See Speed tests.

items.title: Activity
items.text: The reconcile log, newest first. Filter by level, domain or text. Each entry belongs to a numbered pass. Select an entry to see its details, and Show pass #N to see only that pass. Load older gets older entries. The orchestrator keeps the last 10,000 entries in its data directory, so the log continues after a restart.

items.title: Diagnostics
items.text: Container logs and a read-only snapshot of each node. The diagnostics bundle also shows as a report: one verdict for each section. See Diagnostics and troubleshooting.

items.title: Config
items.text:
The page shows:

  • The diff between the desired state and the actual state.
  • Each referenced secret, as present or missing. The page never shows the values.
  • The effective desired state.
  • The config file.

Manage locations opens the Locations page over it. See Maps and locations.

items.title: Node checks
items.text:
The Nodes page shows these checks:

Check What it shows ssh If the orchestrator can reach the node over SSH. docker If Docker is on the node. One check for each container running, with its Docker health in parentheses. starting is degraded, and unhealthy is down. gerbil-udp If Gerbil answers on 51820/udp. pangolin-api The Pangolin API probe: the time of a request through the node to the Integration API of Pangolin. Over 300 ms is degraded. tunnel If the homelab site on the node is online, with the Newt version. mode In dry run, it shows that HomeGAP does no remote access. cluster-proxy In cluster mode, where HAProxy sends PostgreSQL and Valkey. See Cluster database. ee-license The state of the EE license.

items.title: Banners
items.text:
The dashboard shows a banner in these cases:

  • Changes are paused. The banner has Resume.
  • A node update fails and holds the rollout. See Node updates and rollback.
  • Two or more nodes are configured, and none of them answers over SSH. The banner tells you that the homelab lost every node. The log records the start and the end. The nodes continue to serve.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: The Documentation link at the bottom of the menu opens these docs at /docs/, for the version that runs.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text:
This page tells you what happens when a part of the system fails, and how to recover. The orchestrator is never in the traffic path. Thus most failures of the control plane do not affect live traffic.

Failure Effect Recovery A regional node is down. Bunny removes it. Its viewers resolve to the next-nearest node. The orchestrator repairs or provisions the node again. DNS recovers by itself. A node update fails. HomeGAP rolls that node back to its previous stack. The rollout to the other nodes stops. Click Retry update or Skip update, or change the config. See Node updates and rollback. The orchestrator is down. Live traffic does not change. Only new label or config changes wait. Restart the orchestrator. It reconciles to the desired state. The homelab origin is down. Public services are down, because the homelab is the single origin. Passthrough sites show a "back shortly" page (503) approximately 15 seconds after the nodes lose the homelab. Raw ports and resources that the node terminates fail. Restore the origin. The tunnels connect again. The homelab origin is down, in cluster mode. Pangolin apps stay connected. New sign-ins work after approximately 30 seconds, when the nodes elect a database primary. Only the homelab services are not reachable. Restore the origin. The primary moves back after the hold. The node with the database primary is down (cluster). Sign-ins and changes stop for approximately 30 seconds, while the other members elect a new primary. DNS moves public traffic as for any node. Automatic. The primary returns to the homelab after the hold. The homelab is up, but cut off from the nodes (cluster). The homelab loses the vote and stops all writes. The nodes elect a primary and continue to serve. Repair the link. The homelab joins again as a replica and rewinds the writes that it cannot keep. The primary moves back after the hold. The mesh link between two nodes is broken (cluster). Nothing is visible while a majority of members still reach each other. The dashboard shows the isolated member. Repair the network. WireGuard connects again by itself. Fewer than half of the cluster members are reachable. The cluster cannot elect a primary. Sign-ins and changes fail. Connected apps and public traffic continue to work. Bring the members back. The dashboard shows "no majority". The homelab restarts, and the orchestrator starts before the app containers. HomeGAP keeps the services of each container that is gone for reconcile.removal_grace. The containers start, and nothing changes. The teardown of a removed node fails. The node stays on the Nodes page as "teardown failed". Its stack can still run. Decommission the node again, or forget it. See Manage nodes. A Newt tunnel drops. The health probe of that node fails, so Bunny removes the node from DNS. The tunnel supervisor restarts Newt with a backoff. Failover covers the gap. A new record is not on every Bunny nameserver yet. Lookups that go to that nameserver get the answer of the wildcard, which is any node. For a new node, its management host and its status and speed test addresses can go to another node. The tunnels are not affected, because their addresses are pinned. The DNS page shows the record as not in sync, with the answer of each nameserver. HomeGAP checks again on every pass. If the record does not arrive, save it again in the Bunny dashboard or contact Bunny. A Newt connector logs in to another server. The tunnel of that node stays down. Newt retries on the same connection, so it does not recover by itself. After 5 failed logins (approximately 15 seconds), the tunnel supervisor restarts Newt. The Tunnels page shows the reason. The order of the certificate of the nodes fails. The nodes keep the certificate that they have. A node without one shows a certificate warning for the names that it terminates. Read the error in the activity log. See Certificates. The dashboard shows the expiry. See Certificates. A login blocker on a node (fail2ban, sshguard or CrowdSec) bans the orchestrator. SSH from the orchestrator times out, or the server cuts it before login. Setup or provisioning for that node fails. Remove the ban from the console of the provider or from another network. Then try again. The add-node wizard exempts the address of the orchestrator from these blockers. The IP address of the orchestrator changes while ssh_allow_from is set. Provisioning and SSH checks fail for those nodes. Live traffic does not change. Open SSH again from the console of the provider (ufw allow <port>/tcp). Then update ssh_allow_from. Bunny has an outage. DNS resolution has problems. None. Bunny is the single dependency that HomeGAP accepts. The state cache is gone. HomeGAP loses the pauses and the update holds. HomeGAP reads the secrets from the nodes again, creates new API keys and recovers the Newt credentials from the connector spec. The state cache is there, but HomeGAP cannot read it. HomeGAP uses state.json.bak, the copy from its last start. Without a good copy, the orchestrator does not start. Live traffic does not change. Restore state.json from a backup. To start from an empty state, delete the file. The file cluster/secrets.json is gone or damaged while the cluster runs. The cluster part of each pass fails. HomeGAP does not create new passwords, because the database keeps the old ones. Restore the file from a backup of the data directory.

items.title: Maps and locations
items.text: The dashboard and the public status page have maps of your nodes and your homelab. This page tells you what the maps show and how to set locations.

items.title: Where the maps are
items.text:
These pages have a world map that you can drag and zoom:

  • The Overview, Speed test and Locations pages.
  • The add-node wizard.
  • The public status page.

The maps get nothing from a third party. The orchestrator serves all parts:

  • The map library (MapLibre GL).
  • The styles (Protomaps).
  • The fonts and the icons.
  • The map data from OpenStreetMap, as one PMTiles file of 45 MB, to zoom level 6. This is enough for cities and regions.

The release image includes the tiles. Without them, the maps still show the markers, on a plain background.

items.title: The Overview map
items.text:
The Overview map shows every node and the homelab as markers that pulse in their health color. A marker pulses faster when it is not healthy. Lines go from the homelab to each node, in the color of its tunnel.

When you move the pointer over a node, the map shows details of the node. These are its health, its tunnel, its round trip to the homelab, its provider and its failed checks.

When you zoom out, markers that cover each other move apart into a column, with a short line to their real position. When you zoom in, they go back to their exact locations. The known locations of the catalog never move.

items.title: The other maps
items.text:
On the Speed test map, each line has the latest result between the homelab and the node. Click a node to run its test.

In the add-node wizard, search the known data-center cities, for example "dallas", "london" or "hetzner". The search fills in the place name, the region code and the coordinates. Or click the map: the nearest known city within 50 km gives the point its name.

items.title: The Locations page
items.text:
The Locations page is under Config. It has two parts.

The homelab location tells the maps where the homelab is. Set it on this page, or set homelab.location in the config. The API call is PUT /api/homelab/location. The public status page shows only the region of the homelab.

The catalog lists the known locations. Approximately 100 data-center cities come with HomeGAP, with the providers in each city. You can add your own locations, and edit or hide the locations that come with HomeGAP. HomeGAP keeps your changes in <data_dir>/locations.yml.

items.title: Custom tiles
items.text: To build tiles with more detail, run tools/build-map.sh tiles from the repository, with MAP_MAXZOOM set to a higher zoom level. The script builds the tiles from a Protomaps build. Then set map.tiles to the path of the bigger file.

items.title: Attribution
items.text: Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), through Protomaps.

items.title: Node updates and rollback
items.text: HomeGAP updates the stacks of the nodes one at a time, and it rolls back a failed update. This page tells you how an update works and how to recover from a failure.

items.title: Provisioning in the background
items.text: Provisioning runs in the background. A slow node never delays the health checks, the tunnels or DNS for the other nodes. Examples of a slow node are a first install or a slow Docker download. During provisioning, the node shows provisioning… or updating… on the dashboard.

items.title: A rolling update
items.text:
Some changes alter the stack of nodes that are already healthy. Examples are a new image version, the MTU, the tuning and raw ports. HomeGAP sends such a change to one node at a time:

  1. HomeGAP saves the running stack on the node, in <install_dir>/.homegap-rollback. The copy has every managed file. When the Pangolin image changes, it also has the database of Pangolin, because a newer version migrates it.
  2. HomeGAP updates the node. The node must then pass these checks:
    • The health check of Pangolin.
    • The API bootstrap.
    • The final checks: the UDP ports of Gerbil and the Integration API.
    • If its tunnel is up before the update, the tunnel must connect again.
  3. If a step fails, HomeGAP restores the saved stack and restarts it. The node continues to serve on the old stack.

In cluster mode, the first node that starts a new Pangolin version also saves a dump of the database. If that update fails, the rollback restores the dump.

items.title: A failed update
items.text:
A failed update holds the rollout. HomeGAP does not update other nodes, and the dashboard shows a banner with the error. To recover, do one of these actions:

  • Correct the cause on the node. Then click Retry update. HomeGAP applies the update to that node again.
  • Click Skip update. The node stays on its current stack, and the rollout continues with the other nodes.
  • Change the config. HomeGAP tries the new desired stack on the failed node first, and then on the other nodes. If you revert the change, the failure clears.

items.title: What does not wait
items.text:
New nodes and drift repairs do not wait for a rollout.

If the first provisioning of a node fails, HomeGAP tries again after five minutes. To try again at once, click Re-provision.

The steps on the host (Docker, the firewall and the TCP tuning) are idempotent. HomeGAP does not roll them back.

items.title: Drift
items.text: Every reconcile.node_check_interval (default 5 minutes), HomeGAP checks each node over SSH. It repairs the changes that somebody makes outside HomeGAP. To keep a change that you make by hand, pause the node. See Manage nodes.

items.title: Preview the stack of a node
items.text:
To see the stack that HomeGAP writes to a node, run this command. The output does not show the secrets.

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap render-node na1

items.title: Manage nodes
items.text: This page tells you how to add, remove, re-provision and pause nodes, and how to work on a node by hand.

items.title: Add a region
items.text: Use the add-node wizard, or add an entry to nodes[] in the config. HomeGAP provisions the node and adds it to DNS on the next pass. See Add a node.

items.title: Remove a region
items.text:
1. Remove the node from the config. Or click Remove on the Nodes page, which writes the config again. The DNS records of the node drain on the next pass.
  2. The stack on the node continues to run. In cluster mode, the node stays a member of the cluster. When you are ready, click Decommission.
  3. Type the node id to confirm.

The API call is POST /api/nodes/{id}/decommission?confirm={id}.

Until the decommission, you can undo the removal. The dashboard offers Undo for one day, and you can add the node to the config again. The node stays in the cluster, so it needs no new join.

HomeGAP removes only its own records. In cluster mode, the decommission also does these steps:

  • It removes the homelab site and the exit site of the node from the Pangolin of the cluster.
  • It removes the exit node of the node from the Pangolin of the cluster.
  • It removes the member of the node from the vote before it stops the stack, and deletes its data.

In both modes, the decommission then removes the install directory from the node, with the data and the secrets of the stack. If you add the node again, it starts as a new node.

Warning

A decommission deletes the data of the node. In standalone mode, that includes the Pangolin database of the node.

items.title: If the teardown fails
items.text:
If HomeGAP cannot connect to the node, or a step of the teardown fails, the node stays on the Nodes page with the status "teardown failed". The activity log shows the error. The node is out of the cluster vote, but its stack and its secrets can still be on the server.

  • To try again, click Decommission again.
  • If the server is gone, click Forget node. HomeGAP then removes the node from its list and does not connect to the server. The API call is POST /api/nodes/{id}/decommission?confirm={id}&force=true.

Warning

Forget node leaves the stack and the secrets on a server that still runs. Use it only when the server is deleted at the provider.

items.title: Re-provision a node
items.text:
Click Re-provision on the Nodes page. The API call is POST /api/nodes/{id}/provision.

You can destroy and recreate a VPS safely, because HomeGAP can build each node again from nothing. A rebuilt server has a new host key. In the wizard, click Forget the old host key and retry.

items.title: Pause
items.text:
You can pause at three levels:

  • Everything, with Pause in the header.
  • One node, with Pause on the Nodes page.
  • One service, with Pause on the Services page, or with the label homegap.pause.

HomeGAP observes a paused target, but it never changes it. It keeps the DNS records of paused nodes and services. The API call is POST /api/pause with a body like this:

{"scope": "node", "id": "na1", "paused": true}

The scope is global, node or service.

items.title: The management host
items.text:
Newt and the Pangolin client must reach the Pangolin API of each node. HomeGAP routes https://<management_host>/api/v1 on each node. The default of management_host is pangolin-<id>.<domain>. This name is not part of the wildcard passthrough, and it has its own plain DNS record.

The Pangolin ports 3000, 3002 and 3003 on the node listen only on loopback. By default, the web UI of Pangolin is not public. To open it, use SSH port forwarding:

  1. Open the tunnel: 
    ssh -L 3002:127.0.0.1:3002 deploy@203.0.113.10
  2. Open http://localhost:3002 in your browser.

dashboard_public: true routes the web UI publicly on the management host. In standalone mode, auth: sso and auth: pin need this. See Pangolin sign-in for services.

items.title: Work on a node by hand
items.text:
The stack is in /opt/homegap (pangolin.install_dir). If the management user is in the docker group, it can run docker compose there.

Caution

A change that you make by hand is drift. HomeGAP repairs it on the next node check. To keep the change, pause the node first.

items.title: When the homelab loses every node
items.text:
If two or more nodes are configured and none of them answers over SSH, the dashboard shows a banner. The log records the start and the end. The nodes continue to serve. If the outage continues, the nodes also fail the database over.

If the mesh probes show that the nodes reach each other during all of the outage, the problem is in the connection of the homelab.

items.title: Tunnel slots
items.text:
Each node gets a permanent tunnel slot, which the orchestrator keeps in its state. The slot sets these values:

  • The tunnel subnet, 100.89.<128 + 4·slot>.0/22.
  • The kernel interface, hgnewt<slot>.
  • The local ports.

Thus connectors for several nodes can run together in the tunnels container. A new node takes the lowest free slot. A removal or a new order of nodes never moves another node.

Pangolin fixes the subnet when a node registers its exit node for the first time. The orchestrator compares the slot of each node with its live site subnet.

Caution

If two nodes share a subnet, HomeGAP reports an error. This can occur when both nodes are older than tunnel slots. Before you enable tunnels.native, create the Pangolin database of one of the nodes again.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Each request crosses two TCP legs (viewer to node, and node to homelab) and one WireGuard tunnel. This page tells you which settings have the largest effect on throughput.

items.title: The three main settings
items.text: Setting Effect pangolin.tcp_tuning: true (default) Writes /etc/sysctl.d/99-homegap.conf on each node. See TCP tuning on the nodes. tunnels.mtu: 1420 Sets the WireGuard MTU on both ends: Newt --mtu and Gerbil --mtu. The upstream default of 1280 decreases throughput. tunnels.native: true Runs each main tunnel of Newt on a kernel WireGuard interface, instead of the userspace network stack of Newt. This gives the largest gain in most setups.

items.title: TCP tuning on the nodes
items.text:
The file sets BBR congestion control, the fq qdisc, socket buffers up to 64 MiB, MTU probing and a higher tolerance for reordering. BBR keeps long paths with packet loss fast.

Docker containers do not inherit the TCP settings of the host. Thus HomeGAP also applies the same settings in the network namespace of Gerbil and Traefik on the node. The Nodes page shows them as edge tcp.

The node fact tcp_cc shows the congestion control that the kernel really uses. Some VPS kernels refuse BBR.

items.title: The MTU
items.text:
If the path has PPPoE or another tunnel, use a lower MTU. To check a value, run this command from the homelab. Replace <mtu - 28> with the MTU minus 28:

ping -M do -s <mtu - 28> 203.0.113.10

items.title: Native mode
items.text:
With tunnels.native: true, the tunnels container needs:

  • cap_add: [NET_ADMIN].
  • devices: ["/dev/net/tun:/dev/net/tun"].
  • WireGuard in the kernel of the host.

items.title: The homelab side in native mode
items.text:
In native mode, tune the tunnels container itself. TCP settings apply to each network namespace, so the /etc/sysctl.d of the host does not reach containers. The defaults (cubic and a 4 MiB send buffer) limit every download from the homelab to a distant node.

Set the sysctls on the tunnels service:

sysctls:
  net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control: bbr   # needs `modprobe tcp_bbr` on the host
  net.ipv4.tcp_rmem: "4096 131072 67108864"
  net.ipv4.tcp_wmem: "4096 65536 67108864"
  net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle: "0"
  net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing: "1"
  net.ipv4.tcp_reordering: "10"          # tolerate reordering on long routes
  net.ipv4.tcp_max_reordering: "1000"

Caution

For bbr, the host must load the tcp_bbr module (modprobe tcp_bbr). Without it, the container does not start.

To check the settings, run this command:

docker compose exec tunnels sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control net.ipv4.tcp_wmem

On a path with a round trip of approximately 170 ms, these settings took one setup from approximately 115 Mbps to approximately 250 Mbps.

Also enable fq on the host (net.core.default_qdisc = fq). BBR uses it for pacing.

items.title: Userspace mode
items.text: In userspace mode, Newt uses its own TCP stack, so these settings do not apply. A higher net.core.rmem_max and net.core.wmem_max on the host (for example 7500000) still helps its UDP socket.

items.title: Measure the result
items.text: To measure the throughput through the real path, use the speed tests. See Speed tests.

items.title: Speed tests
items.text: The speed tests measure the latency and the throughput through the real traffic path. This page tells you how to enable them and what each test measures.

items.title: Enable the speed tests
items.text:
With speedtest.enabled: true, the orchestrator serves a speed test origin on speedtest.bind. The speed tests need a front door.

Key Default speedtest.enabled false speedtest.hostname speedtest speedtest.bind 0.0.0.0:8089 speedtest.link_ttl 2h speedtest.phase_seconds 8 speedtest.link_budget_gb 20 speedtest.streams 4

A change of speedtest.enabled or speedtest.bind needs a restart of the orchestrator.

The front door already forwards speedtest-<node>.<domain> from the nodes. A node answers the shared name speedtest.<domain> itself, and sends its requests on to the homelab as speedtest-<node>.<domain>. Route these names to the orchestrator on port 8089 from the homelab Traefik. Put these labels on the homegap-mesh service, because it owns the networks of the orchestrator:

labels:
  traefik.enable: "true"
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.rule: "Host(`speedtest.example.net`) || HostRegexp(`^speedtest-[a-z0-9-]+\\.example\\.net$`)"
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.entrypoints: websecure
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.tls: "true"
  traefik.http.services.homegap-speedtest.loadbalancer.server.port: "8089"

If you also enable the status page, use one rule for both. See Status page.

items.title: The two tests
items.text: The Speed test page has two tests. Each test measures ping, jitter, download and upload.

items.title: Homelab ↔ node
items.text:
The orchestrator runs curl on the node over SSH, against port 443 of the node, with the speed test hostname of the node. Thus the traffic takes the production path through the tunnel.

The test uses speedtest.streams parallel streams, and the rates are the sum. One stream shows what a single connection gets over the distance. Several streams show the capacity of the tunnel. You can select the number of streams for each run.

To run the test, click Run test, or click a node on the map. Test all nodes runs the test on each node in turn.

While a test runs, a gauge shows it live: the round trip of each ping, then the download rate, then the upload rate, with a bar for each sample. The speed test origin measures these as the traffic arrives. The final figures come from the node when the test ends.

items.title: Your device → node → homelab
items.text:
This test uses a short-lived link that you open on any device. The link is valid for speedtest.link_ttl.

  1. Click Create test link.
  2. Click Copy.
  3. Open the link on the device.

speedtest.<domain> goes to the node that DNS selects for the device. That node answers the name itself and sends each request on to the homelab under its own name, speedtest-<node>.<domain>.
