The address bar keeps speedtest.<domain>. Thus the page shows the node, and each result belongs to a node. On HTTP, the node redirects to HTTPS on the same name.

The page shows a gauge for each phase as it runs. Test all nodes tests each node in turn through its own name, speedtest-<node>.<domain>, from the same page. Each result belongs to its node. For this, the speed test origin accepts requests from its own pages under any of its names.

The token is in the fragment of the URL. The browser never sends the fragment to a server, so no log contains the token.

A test link has these limits, so that a person with the link cannot use your bandwidth without end:

  • 8 streams at the same time for one link, and 32 streams for all links together.
  • speedtest.link_budget_gb (default 20) GiB of download and upload in total for one link. After that, the link sends and accepts no more data.
  • 20 saved results for one link.

The page uses 4 streams. A test from the homelab to a node has no limit.

items.title: Results
items.text: HomeGAP keeps the results in <data_dir>/speedtests.json. The History panel shows the recent results.

items.title: API
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/speedtest Returns the settings and the recent results. POST /api/speedtest/nodes/{id} Runs a test between the homelab and a node. The call returns when the test ends. GET /api/speedtest/live Returns the running homelab ↔ node test as far as it has got, or 204 when none runs. POST /api/speedtest/link Creates a test link for a device.

items.title: Status page
items.text: The status page is a public page that shows the state of your nodes. This page tells you what it shows, how it works and how to enable it.

items.title: What the page shows
items.text:
With status_page.enabled: true, anybody can open https://status.<domain>/. The page shows:

  • The node that the visitor came through. This is the node that DNS selects for the location of the visitor. The page also shows the round trip of the visitor to the homelab through this node.
  • The state of every node: online, degraded or offline.
  • The round trip of the visitor through each other online node.
State Meaning Online The node works. Degraded The node carries traffic, but a check fails. Offline The node is down, paused or in removal, or its tunnel to the homelab is down.

While the page is open, it refreshes every minute.

The page also has a map of the nodes in their status colors. The node of the visitor is highlighted, with the round trip through each node. The map shows the homelab only as a soft area at the center of its region, for example "Home · North America". HomeGAP never sends the location of the homelab to the page.

items.title: What the page tells a visitor
items.text:
The page and its data are public. For each node, a visitor can read these values:

  • The node id and the region.
  • The state.
  • The location that you set for the node: its name and its coordinates. The map uses them.
  • The name status-<node>.<domain>. The browser measures the round trip through each node on this name. The name resolves to the public address of the node.

The page does not show IP addresses or the management hosts. But a visitor can find the public address of each node from its status-<node> name. The public DNS records of your services give the same addresses.

items.title: Limits on requests
items.text:
The page needs no token, so HomeGAP limits its requests:

  • On the name status.<domain>, each node lets one address send 30 requests in a second, with a burst of 150.
  • The orchestrator lets one address send 1200 requests in a minute to the page, its data and the map. Above that number, it answers 429.

items.title: How the page works
items.text:
Each node answers status.<domain> itself, with its own certificate. This name never goes through passthrough. On HTTP, the node redirects to HTTPS on the same name.

On HTTPS, the node sends each request on to the homelab under its own name, status-<node>.<domain>. That name goes through the front door and the tunnel to the homelab. The address bar keeps status.<domain>, and the orchestrator always knows which node the visitor came through. Thus the page, the node list and every ping come from the orchestrator.

For the round trip through each other node, the browser sends one request to status-<node>.<domain>. The request goes through that node and its tunnel to the homelab, and back. The browser measures the time with Resource Timing, from the request to the first byte. Thus the time does not include DNS and the setup of the connection.

items.title: Enable the status page
items.text:
The status page needs a front door. The first activation needs a restart of the orchestrator.

Key Default Rules status_page.enabled false status_page.hostname status A single lowercase label. status_page.title Status 60 characters or fewer.

items.title: Routing
items.text:
The status page uses the listener of the speed test, speedtest.bind. Thus route status-<node>.<domain> to port 8089 too. When both features are enabled, one rule covers both. Put the labels on the orchestrator service:

labels:
  traefik.enable: "true"
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.rule: "Host(`speedtest.example.net`) || HostRegexp(`^(speedtest|status)-[a-z0-9-]+\\.example\\.net$`)"
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.entrypoints: websecure
  traefik.http.routers.homegap-speedtest.tls: "true"
  traefik.http.services.homegap-speedtest.loadbalancer.server.port: "8089"

To put the homelab on the map, set its location on the Locations page. See Maps and locations.

items.title: Diagnostics and troubleshooting
items.text: This page tells you where to find logs and diagnostics, and what to check for common problems.

items.title: The Diagnostics page
items.text:
The Diagnostics page shows the logs of any container on a node. It also runs a read-only diagnostics bundle. The bundle has:

  • The containers, and the backends of the cluster proxy.
  • The mesh interface and the probe.
  • The addresses, the routes and the Docker networks.
  • The listening ports, the firewall, and the NAT and forwarding rules.
  • The connection tracking, the kernel messages and the recent logs.

You can download the logs and the bundle as text. Nothing on the node changes, and the output contains no secrets.

  1. Select the Node.
  2. Select the Container.
  3. Set Since.
  4. Click Show logs, or click Run diagnostics.
  5. Optional: click Download.

items.title: Log services
items.text:
Service Container pangolin, gerbil, traefik The Pangolin stack. haproxy, db, valkey, sentinel, etcd The cluster member. probe The mesh probe. newt The exit connector.

The API calls are GET /api/nodes/{id}/logs?service=&since=&tail= and GET /api/nodes/{id}/diagnostics. The default of since is 30m. The default of tail is 300 lines, and the maximum is 5000.

items.title: Logs on the homelab
items.text:
Use these commands in the HomeGAP folder:

docker compose logs -f orchestrator
docker compose logs -f tunnels

With HOMEGAP_DEBUG=1, the orchestrator prints stack traces for fatal errors.

items.title: Other pages
items.text:
• The Activity page shows the reconcile log, grouped by domain (GET /api/log?domain=).
  • The Config page shows the diff between the desired state and the actual state (GET /api/diff).

items.title: Problems and checks
items.text: Problem What to check HomeGAP ignores a label. The errors and warnings on the Services page. Look for an unknown label, or a hostname that two containers claim. See Services. A node stays provisioning…. The Activity log and the ssh check. HomeGAP tries a failed first provisioning again after 5 minutes. SSH times out, or the server cuts it before login. A login blocker (fail2ban, sshguard or CrowdSec) can ban the orchestrator. Remove the ban from the console of the provider. Also check ssh_allow_from against the public IP address of the orchestrator. A name does not resolve to the nearest node. The monitor state on the DNS page. Failover takes 1 to 5 minutes. One node cannot fail over. A node is not in the wildcard set. The ee-license check. terminate on the front door needs an EE license on every node. http://<node ip>/ returns 502. The origin is down. http://<node ip>/ times out. The tunnel is down. Look at the Tunnels page. Downloads over long paths are slow. See Performance. cluster-proxy is yellow or red. See Cluster database. A handshake is missing in the Cluster mesh panel. The firewall of the provider must open cluster.mesh.port/udp. A private name returns 403 on the VPN. See Client addresses and private-only services. The orchestrator stops at the start with a homegap: ... error. The config is not valid. Run homegap validate. See Configuration.

items.title: Undo a first test
items.text:
To remove a test installation:

  1. Set reconcile.dry_run: true. This stops all further changes.
  2. In the Bunny console, remove the records with the comment managed-by:homegap.
  3. Restore your previous records.
  4. On the homelab, stop the HomeGAP services: 
    docker compose down
  5. On each node, stop the stack: 
    cd /opt/homegap && sudo docker compose down

items.title: Upgrade the homelab
items.text: Use deploy/upgrade.sh to upgrade HomeGAP on the homelab. The script keeps access up during the upgrade. This page tells you what the script does and how to use it.

items.title: Run the script
items.text:
Put upgrade.sh next to your compose file. Use it instead of docker compose pull && docker compose up -d:

./upgrade.sh

The script gives its arguments to every docker compose call. If your compose file has a different name, give it as an argument:

./upgrade.sh -f homelab-compose.yml
Option What it does --tunnels Recreates the tunnels container, also if its version does not change. --no-pull Uses the images that are already on the host. -h, --help Shows the help.

items.title: Check the image signatures
items.text:
The release build signs the homegap image and the homegap-cluster image with cosign. A signature shows that the build workflow of the HomeGAP repository made the image. The check is optional, and HomeGAP does not do it for you.

To check an image before an upgrade:

  1. Install cosign on the homelab.

  2. Do the check for the homegap image:

    cosign verify ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap:latest \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/DrewCarlson/HomeGAP/\.github/workflows/build\.yml@refs/tags/v'

  3. Do the same check for ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap-cluster:latest.

If the image has a signature from a release build, the command shows the signature and exits with 0. If the command fails, do not run the upgrade.

items.title: What the script does
items.text:
1. It pulls the new images.
  2. It recreates the orchestrator. Traffic never goes through the orchestrator, so this does not stop access. The script waits up to 120 seconds for the orchestrator to start. Then it recreates the mesh agent.
  3. It moves the database primary and the Valkey primary to a node, and holds them there (homegap maintenance start --minutes 30).
  4. It recreates the cluster containers of the homelab one at a time. It waits up to 5 minutes for each container to serve again.
  5. It recreates the tunnel connectors, but only if their code or Newt is different.
  6. It ends the hold (homegap maintenance end). The primaries return to the homelab after the switch-back delay of the cluster.

If the script cannot move the primaries, it stops and does not touch the cluster containers. Correct the cause and run the script again.

If the orchestrator or a cluster container does not serve with its new image, the script restores the previous image of that service. Then it stops. The services after it keep their previous image. The script restores the image with a tag: it gives the previous image the image name of the compose file. A later docker compose pull gets the new image again.

If the service does not serve with its previous image either, the script stops and shows the last lines of its log.

When the script stops early, it ends the hold. The primaries then return to the homelab when its member is healthy again. If the start of the maintenance fails, HomeGAP removes the hold at once.

items.title: The mesh container
items.text: The script never recreates homegap-mesh. The mesh and every container in its network namespace restart with it. The script does recreate homegap-mesh-agent. The mesh interface stays up without the agent.

items.title: The tunnels container
items.text:
The tunnels container restarts every Newt connector at once. Thus every node loses the homelab for a few seconds.

The script recreates it only when the tunnels version of the new image is different. This version covers the code of the tunnel supervisor, its platform layer, the dependency versions and Newt. The script also recreates it when it does not run, or with --tunnels.

Until then, the container continues to run the previous image. Thus Docker also keeps that image.

items.title: Merged compose projects
items.text:
If the HomeGAP services are part of a different compose project with other names, set these environment variables:

Variable Default HG_ORCHESTRATOR orchestrator HG_TUNNELS tunnels HG_CLUSTER homegap-etcd:etcd homegap-sentinel:sentinel homegap-valkey:valkey homegap-db:patroni

HG_CLUSTER is a list of service:role pairs, separated by spaces, in the order of the restarts.

items.title: Standalone mode
items.text:
The script asks the orchestrator to start maintenance only if the compose file has cluster services. In standalone mode, the orchestrator answers that the cluster is not enabled. The script pulls the images of the cluster containers, but it does not recreate them. It does not end a hold. It still updates the orchestrator and the tunnels.

If the compose file has no cluster services, the script skips the cluster steps.

items.title: After the upgrade
items.text:
After the upgrade, the cluster members on the nodes follow the cluster image of the homelab, pinned to its registry digest. HomeGAP updates one node in each pass, and only while every member serves and no maintenance runs. See Cluster database.

The script does not update the node stacks (the Pangolin images). They follow the config. See Node updates and rollback.

items.title: HTTP API
items.text: The dashboard uses an HTTP API on the orchestrator. You can use the same API from scripts. This page lists every route.

items.title: Basics
items.text:
The base URL is http://<dashboard.bind>. Every /api/* route needs the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. The token comes from dashboard.auth_token_env or dashboard.auth_token_file. Without them, HomeGAP creates a token. See Dashboard.

An action returns {"ok": true, "message": "..."}. An error returns {"ok": false, "message": "..."}, with one of these HTTP status codes:

Code When 400 The input is not valid. 409 The request conflicts with the current state. 500 Any other error.

Warning

The API has control of every node. Never expose it publicly. See Security model.

items.title: Routes outside /api
items.text:
These routes need no token:

Route What it does GET /healthz Returns ok. GET /map/... The tiles of the map (with range requests), its scripts, its fonts and its icons. The public listener also serves them when the status page is enabled. GET /docs/... These docs. GET /... Any other path returns the dashboard app.

items.title: Status and log
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/status Returns the full status snapshot. GET /api/events?after=SEQ Server-sent events. The status event sends the snapshot when it changes. The log event sends the new log entries after SEQ. GET /api/log?domain=&limit= Returns the recent reconcile log. The default of limit is 300.

items.title: Config
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/config Returns the config file and the nodes. GET /api/diff Returns the items of the diff between desired and actual state, and the effective desired state. GET /api/secrets Returns the referenced secrets: names, sources and presence. It never returns the values.

items.title: Control
items.text: Route What it does POST /api/resync Queues a pass. POST /api/pause Pauses or resumes. Body: {"scope": "global", "id": null, "paused": true}. The scope is global, node or service. POST /api/cluster/switchover Makes a caught-up replica the database primary now. Body: {"to": "<member>"}. Cluster only. POST /api/cluster/maintenance/start?minutes=N Moves the cluster primaries off the homelab and holds them for up to N minutes (default 30). POST /api/cluster/maintenance/end Ends the hold.

items.title: Nodes
items.text: Route What it does POST /api/nodes Adds a node. The body is a node entry. HomeGAP writes the config file again, with a backup. DELETE /api/nodes/{id} Removes a node from the config. DNS drains first. The stack stays up, and the node stays in the cluster, until the decommission. POST /api/nodes/{id}/provision Queues a full provisioning of the node. POST /api/nodes/{id}/update/retry Applies a held update to the node again. POST /api/nodes/{id}/update/skip Leaves the node on its current stack, and continues the rollout. POST /api/nodes/{id}/decommission?confirm={id} Stops the stack of a removed node and forgets the node. confirm must repeat the node id. If the teardown fails, the call returns an error and the node stays. With force=true, HomeGAP forgets the node without a teardown. GET /api/nodes/{id}/logs?service=&since=&tail= Returns the logs of a container. See Diagnostics and troubleshooting. The default of since is 30m. The default of tail is 300 lines, and the maximum is 5000. GET /api/nodes/{id}/diagnostics Returns the read-only diagnostics bundle of the node: {node, title, text, at}.

items.title: Node setup (the add-node wizard)
items.text: Route What it does POST /api/setup/test Tests an initial SSH login. Body: host, port, user, password or keyFile, and resetHostKey. POST /api/setup/keys Generates, imports or describes the SSH key of a node. Body: nodeId, mode, and privateKey or path. POST /api/setup/jobs Starts a setup job. GET /api/setup/jobs/{id} Returns the progress of a setup job.

items.title: Locations
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/locations Returns the known locations (shipped and local) and the location of the homelab. PUT /api/locations/{id} Adds or edits a location. DELETE /api/locations/{id}?reset= Removes a location. A shipped location becomes hidden. With reset=true, an edited shipped location goes back to the original. PUT /api/homelab/location Sets the location of the homelab. Body: {"location": {"latitude": ..., "longitude": ..., "name": "..."}}, or {"location": null} to clear it.

items.title: Access (cluster only)
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/access Returns the users, roles, open invitations and devices of the cluster. POST /api/access/users Adds a user. Body: {"email": "...", "roleIds": [...], "password": "..."}. Without password, the response has the invite link. DELETE /api/access/users/{id} Removes a user. PUT /api/access/users/{id}/roles Sets the roles of a user. Body: {"roleIds": [...]}. DELETE /api/access/invitations/{id} Withdraws an open invitation. POST /api/access/devices/{id}/{action} Does an action on a device: block, unblock, archive, unarchive or delete.

items.title: Speed test
items.text: Route What it does GET /api/speedtest Returns the settings and the recent results. POST /api/speedtest/nodes/{id}?streams=N Runs a test between the homelab and a node. The call returns when the test ends. streams is optional. POST /api/speedtest/link Creates a test link for a device.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
To read the status, set TOKEN to your dashboard token. Then run this command:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/status

To queue a pass:

curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/resync

To follow the events (after=SEQ continues the log from an entry):

curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/events

items.title: Command line
items.text:
The homegap binary has one command for each role. This page lists the commands, their options and their output.

In the container, run a command with docker compose exec orchestrator homegap <command>. The entrypoint of the image is tini -- homegap, and the default command is run.

items.title: run
items.text:
homegap [run] [--config PATH] [--dry-run] [--once]

Runs the orchestrator. This is the default command.

Option What it does --config PATH The config file. See Configuration. --dry-run Runs in dry run. HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN with 1, true or yes does the same. --once Runs one pass, without the dashboard and the public listener, then stops.

items.title: tunnels
items.text:
homegap tunnels [--dir PATH] [--newt PATH]

Runs the tunnel supervisor. It keeps one Newt connector for each node.

Option Default Environment variable --dir PATH /tunnels HOMEGAP_TUNNELS_DIR --newt PATH /usr/local/bin/newt HOMEGAP_NEWT

items.title: mesh
items.text:
homegap mesh [--dir PATH]

Runs the mesh agent of the homelab. It keeps the mesh interface and the firewall of the namespace that it runs in. See Cluster mesh.

Option Default Environment variable --dir PATH /mesh HOMEGAP_MESH_DIR

items.title: validate
items.text:
homegap validate [--config PATH]

Checks the config file. If the file is valid, the command prints OK: <n> node(s), domain <domain>, zone <zone>. If not, it prints Invalid configuration: and the list of errors.

items.title: plan
items.text:
homegap plan [--config PATH] --labels FILE

Prints the desired state for a set of labels, without Docker. The file is a JSON map of container names to their labels. See Services.

The output has these lines, in this order:

ERROR <container>: ...
WARN  <container>: ...
node <id> (<management host>)
  public  ...
  private ...
  sni     ...
  port    ...
dns <type> <fqdn> -> <value> [<node>] <purpose> [geo] monitor=<monitor>

items.title: render-node
items.text:
homegap render-node ID [--config PATH]

Prints the stack files that HomeGAP writes to a node, with the secrets redacted. The last file is the dynamic routes file.

items.title: maintenance
items.text:
homegap maintenance start [--minutes N] | end

Asks the orchestrator in the same container to move the cluster primaries off the homelab. The orchestrator holds them there for up to N minutes (default 30). end ends the hold. The command uses the dashboard API, with the dashboard token if you set one. See Cluster database.

items.title: version and help
items.text: homegap version (or --version) prints the version of the binary. homegap help (or --help, -h) prints the usage.

items.title: Exit codes and errors
items.text:
Case Result An unknown command. The command prints the usage and exits with code 2. A fatal error. The command prints homegap: <message> on stderr, and homegap: caused by ... if there is a cause. It exits with code 1.

With HOMEGAP_DEBUG set, a fatal error also prints the stack trace.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Variable Default HOMEGAP_CONFIG /config/config.yml HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN None. DOCKER_SOCKET /var/run/docker.sock

For all variables, see the Configuration reference.

items.title: Files and state
items.text: This page lists the files that HomeGAP reads and writes on the homelab and on the nodes.

items.title: The data directory of the orchestrator
items.text:
The data directory is data_dir (default /data), on the homegap-data volume.

Path Content state.json The state cache, with mode 0600. state.json.bak A copy of the state cache from the last start. HomeGAP uses it if state.json is damaged. discovery.json The containers of the last discovery, with their labels. HomeGAP uses it for the grace period of a container that is gone. dashboard-token The dashboard token that HomeGAP creates if the config gives none, with mode 0600. known_hosts The SSH host keys of the nodes. ssh/ The SSH keys that the add-node wizard generates, with mode 0600. ssh-askpass.sh A helper that gives the setup password to ssh. tunnels/ The connector specs, which the tunnels container also reads. With the shipped compose file, this is the homegap-tunnels volume at /tunnels. acme/ The ACME account key, and the certificate of the nodes with its key. See Certificates. cluster/secrets.json The cluster passwords: PostgreSQL, Valkey, Sentinel, etcd and the Patroni API. cluster/homelab-role The role of the homelab that HomeGAP records when it creates the cluster. cluster/backups/ With cluster.homelab_role: vote, the daily dumps of the cluster database. HomeGAP keeps the newest seven. cluster/config/ The configs of the homelab member, which the cluster containers read. With the shipped compose file, this is the homegap-cluster-config volume at /cluster-config. cluster/maintenance The maintenance hold, in cluster mode. mesh/ The description of the mesh for the mesh agent, its status and the mesh key of the homelab. With the shipped compose file, this is the homegap-mesh volume at /mesh. locations.yml Your edits to the location catalog. speedtests.json The results of the speed tests.

items.title: The config file
items.text: The config file is /config/config.yml. Edits from the dashboard leave backups next to it, as config.yml.bak-<epoch ms>. See Configuration.

items.title: The homelab compose folder
items.text: Path Content .env The secrets, with mode 600. secrets/ssh/ The private SSH keys of nodes that you add by hand. backups/ In cluster mode, the nightly pg_dump files. HomeGAP keeps the newest seven.

items.title: The image
items.text:
Path Content /usr/local/bin/homegap The HomeGAP binary. /usr/local/bin/newt The Newt binary. /usr/share/homegap/map/world.pmtiles The map tiles. /usr/share/homegap/docs These docs. /usr/share/homegap/tunnels-version The tunnels version, for deploy/upgrade.sh.

The image creates the system user homegap (uid 10001), with the home directory /data. The Dockerfile has no USER line, so the container runs as root by default.

items.title: The node
items.text:
The stack is in install_dir (default /opt/homegap):

Path Content compose.yml The compose file of the Pangolin stack. .env The environment of the stack, with mode 0600. config/config.yml The Pangolin config, with mode 0600. config/traefik/traefik_config.yml The static config of Traefik. config/traefik/dynamic/homegap-routes.yml The routes that HomeGAP writes. config/traefik/dynamic/homegap-tls.yml The TLS config of Traefik. config/traefik/certs/homegap.crt, homegap.key The certificate from certificates. config/maintenance/ The files of the "back shortly" page. config/homegap-sysctl.conf The TCP tuning. HomeGAP installs it as /etc/sysctl.d/99-homegap.conf. secrets/node.json The secrets of the node, with mode 0600. .homegap-rollback The saved stack, during an update. cluster/ The compose project of the cluster member, in cluster mode. exit/ The exit connector, if exits through nodes are enabled.

HomeGAP also writes these files on the node:

Path Content /etc/sysctl.d/99-homegap.conf The TCP tuning of the host. /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-homegap.conf The SSH hardening from the add-node wizard. /run/homegap-probe The readings of the mesh probe. A reboot clears them.

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
This page defines the terms that the HomeGAP docs use.

Blueprint A Pangolin file that declares resources. HomeGAP applies one blueprint for each resource, and an optional base blueprint. See Pangolin options. Bunny DNS The DNS service of bunny.net. It sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. See DNS routing and health checks. Cluster mode The mode with a cluster: key in the config. All nodes are one Pangolin EE cluster on a shared database. See Cluster mode. Connector A Newt process that connects the homelab to one node through WireGuard. The tunnel supervisor runs one connector for each node. See How HomeGAP works. Desired state The Docker labels and the config file, and nothing else. The orchestrator moves the actual state toward it. See How HomeGAP works. Drift A change on a node that HomeGAP did not make. The node check repairs it. See Node updates and rollback. Exit node An exit to the internet for the Pangolin apps, through a node or through the homelab. See Exit nodes. Front door The homelab Traefik container with the root domain in homegap.expose. It claims the root and, with homegap.wildcard, *.<domain>. See Services. Geo record set A set of DNS records for one name, one for each node, with geo routing and a health monitor. See DNS routing and health checks. Gerbil The WireGuard server of Pangolin on each node. Health resource A resource on each node that sends the Bunny probe through the tunnel to the front door. See Traffic paths. Homelab The home servers with Docker, the homelab Traefik and the services. It has no inbound ports. Management host The name of the Pangolin API of a node, by default pangolin-<id>.<domain>. See Manage nodes. Mesh The private WireGuard network hg-mesh between the homelab and every node, in cluster mode. See Cluster mesh. Named service A service under homegap.services.<name>. on a container that can also have other services. Its key is <host slug>--<name>. See Named services. Newt The tunnel client of Pangolin. HomeGAP runs it on the homelab as connectors. niceId The fixed id of a Pangolin resource. The ids of the resources that HomeGAP manages start with hg-. HomeGAP deletes only stale hg-* resources. Node A VPS that runs Pangolin, Gerbil and Traefik. Node ids are like na1, eu1 and as1. See Prepare the servers. Olm The Pangolin client in the Pangolin apps. Orchestrator The homegap run process on the homelab. It reads the labels and manages the nodes, the tunnels and DNS. It is never in the traffic path. Pangolin EE The Enterprise Edition of Pangolin, by Fossorial. HomeGAP needs it for cluster mode and for wildcard resources in terminate mode. See Pangolin EE licenses. Pass One run of the reconcile loop. See How HomeGAP works. Passthrough The TLS mode where the node reads only the SNI and forwards the encrypted stream to the homelab. See Traffic paths. Port list A list of raw ports in homegap.port, with entries like 7881/tcp, 3478/tcp+udp or 2222:22/tcp. See Port lists. Primary and replica The primary is the database member that accepts writes. A replica follows the primary. See Cluster database. Private path A route that only Pangolin clients use to reach a public service, over a separate Docker network. See Client addresses and private-only services. Private resource A Pangolin resource that only the Pangolin client can reach. See Private services. Rollout An update of the node stacks, one node at a time. See Node updates and rollback. Site A Pangolin object for a network that a connector serves. The homelab has a site on each node. See Clustered Pangolin. Slot The permanent tunnel slot of a node. It sets the tunnel subnet, the interface and the mesh address. See Manage nodes. Standalone mode The mode without a cluster: key. Each node runs its own Pangolin with SQLite. See Standalone or cluster. Switch-back The move of the database primary back to the homelab, after the homelab stays caught up for cluster.primary.switch_back_after. See Cluster database. Terminate The TLS mode where the node ends TLS. Pangolin sign-in needs it. See Traffic paths. Tunnel supervisor The tunnels container (homegap tunnels). It runs one Newt connector for each node. See Install on the homelab. Vote The etcd quorum of the cluster. It needs a majority to elect a primary. See Cluster database.

items.title: Ports and firewall
items.text: This page lists the ports that HomeGAP uses on the nodes and on the homelab.

items.title: Node: public ports
items.text:
With firewall: true (the default), HomeGAP opens these ports in ufw:

Port Use ssh_port/tcp (default 22) SSH, from anywhere or only from ssh_allow_from. 80/tcp HTTP: the health probe of Bunny and the redirects to HTTPS. 443/tcp HTTPS. 443/udp UDP on the HTTPS port. 51820/udp and 21820/udp WireGuard, for Gerbil. cluster.mesh.port/udp (default 51821) The cluster mesh, in cluster mode. The public ports of raw services Raw TCP and UDP services, as their labels set them.

A firewall at the provider level must open the same ports.

items.title: Node: ports on loopback
items.text: Port Use 3000, 3002, 3003 Pangolin. The orchestrator reaches them through SSH port forwarding. 127.0.0.1:8404 The stats page of HAProxy, in cluster mode.

items.title: Node: reserved ports
items.text: The node uses these ports itself: 22, 80, 443, 2379, 2380, 3000, 3001, 3002, 3003, 3004, 3005, 5432, 5433, 6379, 6380, 8008, 8080, 8082, 8090, 21820, 26379 and 51820. A public raw service cannot use them. In cluster mode, it also cannot use cluster.mesh.port/udp.

items.title: Node: internal ports
items.text: Port Use From pangolin.passthrough_port_base (default 40000) The internal proxy ports of passthrough resources. HomeGAP never publishes them. cluster-proxy:5433 PostgreSQL, through HAProxy, on the homegap-cluster network. Cluster mode only. cluster-proxy:6380 Valkey, through HAProxy, on the homegap-cluster network. Cluster mode only.

items.title: Homelab
items.text:
The homelab has no inbound ports from the internet.

Port Use dashboard.bind (8088) The dashboard. Reach it only privately. speedtest.bind (8089) The public origin of the speed test and the status page. Your Traefik routes to it. 8080 on your Traefik The Traefik API, with api.insecure: true, for homegap.private_middleware. Do not publish it.

items.title: Addresses
items.text:
Range Use Host 1 of cluster.mesh.subnet The mesh address of the homelab. Host 10 + slot of cluster.mesh.subnet The mesh address of a node. 100.89.<128 + 4·slot>.0/22 The tunnel subnet of a node.

See Cluster mesh and Manage nodes.

items.title: Security model
items.text: This page tells you where HomeGAP keeps its secrets, what each part can reach and what the public can see.

items.title: The orchestrator is the trust center
items.text:
The orchestrator holds every SSH key and every API key. Thus:

  • Run it on a minimal host.
  • Mount the secrets. Do not put them in the image.
  • Keep the dashboard private. Every /api route needs the dashboard token. Set your own token with dashboard.auth_token_env.

Warning

If somebody gets access to the dashboard or to the orchestrator host, that person has control of every node.

The PIN of a service is never in the data that the dashboard shows.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
HomeGAP creates the secrets of each node from the CSPRNG of the kernel. These are the Pangolin server secret, the admin credentials, the setup token and the CrowdSec bouncer key. It sends them over SSH to <install_dir>/secrets/node.json (mode 0600). This file is the source of truth. The local state file /data/state.json (mode 0600) is only a cache. If you lose it, HomeGAP reads the credentials from the node again.

The add-node wizard keeps a setup password in memory for the job only. It never stores it. HomeGAP writes generated node keys to the data directory with mode 0600.

See Secrets.

items.title: Access to the nodes
items.text:
On each node, the Pangolin API key of the orchestrator is a root key, restricted to the actions that HomeGAP needs. HomeGAP retires its older keys by itself.

The Pangolin ports 3000, 3002 and 3003 on the node listen only on loopback. The orchestrator reaches them only through SSH port forwarding.

ufw on the node opens only the ports in Ports and firewall. HomeGAP adds new rules before it removes its old rules. It never touches rules that it did not add.

items.title: The homelab
items.text:
The orchestrator has no Docker socket. It reads Docker through the docker-proxy service, which accepts only GET requests for the container list, the events and the image data. Only the orchestrator can reach the proxy. The tunnels run in a separate container. Thus the orchestrator never carries traffic.

The orchestrator runs with two capabilities: NET_ADMIN for its route to the mesh, and DAC_OVERRIDE to read the mounted keys and config.

Warning

Do not mount the Docker socket in the orchestrator. A socket mount gives the full Docker API, also with :ro. A person who controls that container then controls the Docker host.

Only the orchestrator mounts the homegap-data volume, which holds the state cache, the SSH keys and the dashboard token. The cluster containers and the tunnels container each mount only their own volume.

In cluster mode, Pangolin on each node uses its own database role, pangolin. This role owns the pangolin database and is not a superuser. The superuser postgres can sign in only from inside a member, never over the mesh.

The containers of a node cannot control the cluster. etcd and Sentinel need a password that Pangolin does not hold. A firewall on each node keeps its containers away from the etcd peer port and the Sentinel port. See Cluster mesh.

Each node also votes in the cluster database. Patroni members share their config, so a person with root on a node can still run commands in the cluster containers of the homelab. HomeGAP therefore isolates those containers:

  • They are in their own network namespace, without the orchestrator. A firewall there lets them open connections only on the mesh. They cannot reach the dashboard, your other containers or your home network.
  • They mount the cluster database and their own config, and nothing else of the orchestrator.

See Cluster mesh.

To have no database member on the homelab, set cluster.homelab_role: vote. Then the homelab only votes, and the database is on the nodes. See The homelab as a vote only.

HomeGAP never publishes the IP address of the homelab. Every tunnel goes outbound from home. In cluster mode, the homelab dials the mesh. On the homelab end of the mesh, HomeGAP drops inbound traffic, except replies, ping and the ports of the cluster database.

The add-node wizard sends a password only to a host key that you confirmed. After that, HomeGAP connects to a node only if it shows the host key from its first connection.

items.title: Images
items.text:
The default images of the node stack have a version tag. A node gets a new version only when the default or your config changes. See Node updates and rollback.

The release build signs the HomeGAP images. HomeGAP does not check a signature before it uses an image. To check the images yourself, see Check the image signatures.

items.title: Traffic
items.text:
With passthrough, a node cannot read the traffic. It holds no certificate for a passthrough name. With the CAA records of the domain, it cannot order one. A node can see the name, the address of the client, and the size and time of the traffic.

A node can read the traffic of each name that it terminates. These are its own Pangolin, the shared names of the status page and the speed test, and each service with homegap.tls: terminate. A front door with terminate and homegap.wildcard gives the nodes all web traffic of the domain. See Certificates.

The nodes send an HSTS header on each name that they terminate. A browser then uses only HTTPS for that name for one year.

pangolin.crowdsec gives abuse mitigation on the edge for terminated traffic only. It cannot examine passthrough streams.

items.title: Calls to outside services
items.text:
The software that HomeGAP runs makes no calls home of its own. HomeGAP turns off:

  • Pangolin: its usage data, the product news and newest-version notices on its dashboard, and the download of its AI model catalog. It reads an empty catalog from its config instead.
  • Traefik on the nodes: its version check and its usage data.

Some calls have no setting. In the container that makes the call, HomeGAP resolves the name to 127.0.0.1, so the call fails on the machine itself:

  • Newt asks api.fossorial.io for the newest version each time it starts. This affects the tunnels container on the homelab and each node's exit connector.
  • Pangolin looks up its public address at checkip.amazonaws.com, ifconfig.io and api.ipify.org each time it starts. The address only fills in a hint on the DNS records page of its dashboard, and HomeGAP publishes the DNS records of each node itself.

The calls that remain are needed for the system to work:

  • If you use a Pangolin EE license key, the nodes check it at api.fossorial.io.
  • Traefik on the nodes downloads its plugins (Pangolin's badger, and the CrowdSec bouncer if enabled) from the Traefik plugin catalog when it starts.
  • The orchestrator orders the certificate of the nodes from Let's Encrypt. The nodes order no certificates.
  • With pangolin.crowdsec, CrowdSec talks to its central API for the community blocklists.

Your own Traefik on the homelab is configured by you. Set global.checkNewVersion and global.sendAnonymousUsage to false in its static configuration to turn off the same calls there.

items.title: What the public can see
items.text:
• The public status page shows the id, the region, the state and the location of each node. It also uses the name status-<node>.<domain> of each node, which resolves to the public address of that node. It shows the homelab only as its region. See Status page.
  • The token of a speed test link for a device is in the fragment of the URL. The browser never sends it to a server, so no log contains it. See Speed tests.
  • The nodes end TLS for the shared names status.<domain> and speedtest.<domain>, which serve only these HomeGAP pages. A node then sends each request back into its own port 443 under its own name, and the front door carries it home still encrypted. On that inner connection the node does not check the certificate, because the connection does not leave the node before it enters the tunnel.

items.title: Report a security issue
items.text: To report a security issue, open a private security advisory on GitHub at https://github.com/DrewCarlson/HomeGAP/security/advisories/new. Do not open a public issue.

items.title: Services
items.text: This page tells you how HomeGAP publishes the services of your homelab, and when a service needs its own labels.

items.title: Labels are the source of truth
items.text: The orchestrator reads the homegap.* labels of your containers from Docker. It reads through the docker-proxy service, which refuses each request that changes something. The orchestrator never writes labels. When a container starts, stops or changes, the Docker event starts a pass at once. The debounce is reconcile.debounce (default 2s).

items.title: Most services need no labels
items.text:
The front door carries every name under your domain. The front door is the homelab Traefik container with the root domain in homegap.expose and homegap.wildcard: "true". To publish a service through the front door, add a normal Traefik router at home.

HomeGAP treats a service as the front door when its homegap.expose is equal to domain and its access is public. A raw service is never the front door.

items.title: When a service needs labels
items.text:
Label a container only when it needs its own path:

  • A dedicated hostname. The service gets its own resource and its own DNS record set. This resource has priority over the wildcard. See Traffic paths.
  • Raw TCP or UDP ports. See Raw TCP and UDP.
  • A private service, for Pangolin clients only. See Private services.
  • Pangolin sign-in in front of the service. See Pangolin sign-in for services.
  • Only some of the nodes serve the service. Use homegap.regions for this.

For all labels, see the Label reference. For the real addresses of viewers and for services that only Pangolin clients can open, see Client addresses and private-only services.

items.title: Several services on one container
items.text: One container can declare more than one service, with named services under homegap.services.<name>.. For example, a voice server can have a port list on one name and a second service with a different public port. See Named services.

items.title: Who can claim a hostname
items.text:
Only one http or https service can claim a hostname. If two containers have the same homegap.expose, the first container in the order of names wins. Each other container gets this error:

hostname <name> is already claimed by <container>

Raw services can share a hostname with each other, and with one http or https service. On the nodes that they share, only one public service can use a public port and protocol. See Shared hostnames and ports.

items.title: How the tunnel finds the container
items.text: The tunnel connects to the container by its name, or by the value of homegap.host. The name must resolve on a Docker network that the container shares with the tunnels container.

items.title: When a container is gone
items.text:
When a container with homegap.* labels stops, HomeGAP keeps its services for reconcile.removal_grace (default 3 minutes). After that time, HomeGAP removes the resources and the DNS records of the container.

The grace period prevents a short outage after a restart of the homelab. The orchestrator can start before your app containers. Without the grace period, HomeGAP removes each service and creates it again a moment later.

A new container that claims the same hostname immediately replaces the container that is gone. If the orchestrator cannot list the containers at all, it uses the containers of the last list until Docker answers again.

items.title: Errors and warnings
items.text:
The Services page on the dashboard and the log show the label errors of each container. HomeGAP does not publish a service with errors. The errors of one container never stop the other services. The errors of a named service start with services.<name>:, and they drop only that service.

A warning does not stop the publication of the service. An unknown homegap.* label gives this warning, and HomeGAP ignores the label:

unknown label '<key>' ignored

items.title: Preview the result of labels
items.text:
The homegap plan command shows what a set of labels produces, without Docker. The input is a JSON file that maps each container name to its labels:

{
  "traefik": {
    "homegap.expose": "example.net",
    "homegap.wildcard": "true",
    "homegap.protocol": "https"
  }
}

The orchestrator process must be able to read the file. If you put the file in the config/ folder next to config.yml and mount it at /config/labels.json, run this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap plan --labels /config/labels.json

The output starts with the ERROR and WARN lines. Then, for each node, it shows the public, private, sni and port items. The dns records come last.

Note

homegap plan does not read Docker networks or the Traefik API. Thus a front door with homegap.private_network or homegap.private_middleware gives errors in the plan output. These errors do not apply to the orchestrator, which reads both.

items.title: Pangolin sign-in for services
items.text: Pangolin can ask for a sign-in or a PIN before a viewer reaches a service. This page tells you how to enable this with labels.

items.title: The two modes
items.text:
homegap.auth: sso puts the Pangolin sign-in in front of the service. homegap.roles lists the roles that can open it. The Admin role can always open it.

homegap.auth: pin asks for a 6-digit PIN. The PIN comes from the environment variable that homegap.pin_env names, on the orchestrator. Docker secrets also work, through /run/secrets/<NAME>.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Both modes need homegap.tls: terminate, because the node cannot authenticate encrypted traffic. On the front door, terminate with a wildcard needs Pangolin EE. See Traffic paths.

The sign-in pages must be public:

StandaloneCluster

Set dashboard_public: true on each node. Then the node routes its Pangolin web UI on its management host, pangolin-<id>.<domain>.

The links and redirects of Pangolin use the client address pangolin.<domain>. Every node serves the login pages and the API on this address. You do not set anything more.

items.title: Users
items.text:
In standalone mode, you manage the users in the Pangolin UI of each node. In cluster mode, you manage them on the Access page. See Users and devices.

The resources of the speed test and the status page never have sign-in. HomeGAP creates them without it.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A service on its own hostname, with Pangolin sign-in for the Member role:

grafana:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "grafana.example.net"
    homegap.protocol: "https"
    homegap.tls: "terminate"
    homegap.auth: "sso"
    homegap.roles: "Member"

items.title: Client addresses and private-only services
items.text: This page tells you how to give the homelab the real address of each viewer. It also tells you how to make a Traefik allowlist that only Pangolin clients pass. The result is like Cloudflare WARP with two tunnels, but with one container.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Every connection reaches the homelab from the tunnels container. Thus the homelab Traefik sees one address for all viewers. Two labels on the front door solve this:

  • homegap.proxy_protocol sends the real address of each public viewer.
  • homegap.private_network sends the traffic of Pangolin clients from a separate network.

items.title: Real client addresses
items.text:
With homegap.proxy_protocol: "true" on the front door, the node adds a PROXY protocol v2 header to the encrypted stream. TLS stays passthrough, and the node reads only the SNI name.

The Pangolin TCP resource gets proxy-protocol: true, version 2. Standalone nodes get the transport pp-transport-v2 from the routes file of HomeGAP. Clustered nodes use the definition of Pangolin.

The homelab Traefik must trust the header only from the tunnels container. Give tunnels a fixed address on the traefik network, for example 172.32.0.250. Then trust that address on the entrypoint:

entryPoints:
  websecure:
    proxyProtocol:
      trustedIPs: ["172.32.0.250/32"]

Connections without the header from a trusted address continue to work, for example from your LAN and from the health probes of the nodes. Terminated services get X-Forwarded-For instead. To trust it, add forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs with the same address.

Caution

If you add the label before the entrypoint trusts the header, every TLS handshake through the nodes fails. Configure the entrypoint first.

items.title: Private-only services
items.text:
With homegap.private_network: "homegap-private", HomeGAP uses a second Docker network that only tunnels and the front door share. Compose adds the project name to the start of the names of project networks. Thus HomeGAP matches a network with exactly the name in the label, or a name that ends in _<label>.

Pangolin clients resolve each private name to a private resource with these settings:

  • The destination is the address of the front door on the private network.
  • The ports are homegap.port (443 by default), plus 80 for https.
  • The roles come from homegap.roles.
  • The niceId is hg-private--<slug of the name>.

The connection leaves tunnels from the private network. Thus the homelab Traefik sees it come from that subnet, and public traffic never has an address in that range. On the private-only routers, accept only that range and your LAN:

http:
  middlewares:
    private-only:
      ipAllowList:
        sourceRange: ["172.33.0.0/24", "192.168.1.0/24"]

Put the middleware on the routers of the private-only services, in labels or in the files of Traefik.

items.title: Public traffic never uses the private network
items.text:
The tunnels container is on both networks. Thus Docker DNS can answer the container name with the private address. To prevent this, HomeGAP sends public traffic to the address of the front door on its other network, unless you set homegap.host.

HomeGAP gives an error in these cases:

Case Result The front door is only on the private network. An error. Public traffic needs another network that the front door shares with tunnels. The front door is on more than one other network. An error. Set homegap.host to the address of the front door on the network that it shares with tunnels. The front door has no address on the named network. An error. HomeGAP leaves out only the private path. Public traffic does not change.

items.title: Which names get a private path
items.text:
Two labels select the names:

  • homegap.private_hosts gives a list of names.
  • homegap.private_middleware finds the names from the routers of Traefik.

You can use the two labels together or one of them alone.

items.title: Find the names from the routers
items.text:
With homegap.private_middleware: "private-only@file", HomeGAP reads the routers of this Traefik from its API (/api/http/routers, all pages). It reads only this Traefik. It never reads another Traefik on the host.

Each name in a Host(...) rule of an enabled router that uses the middleware gets a private path. HomeGAP compares the middleware without its @provider part. These rules apply:

  • A name outside the hostname of the front door gets a warning and no private path.
  • HomeGAP cannot read the names of a router with HostRegexp, or of a router without Host. It gives a warning. List those names in homegap.private_hosts.

A service in a subfolder of the root gives the root its private path. An example is a router with Host(`example.net`) && PathPrefix(`/grafana`). Pangolin clients then reach the whole root over the private network. Its public routers continue to answer them.

items.title: The Traefik API
items.text:
The orchestrator must be able to reach the API of Traefik on the traefik network. With api.insecure: true in the static config of Traefik, the API answers on port 8080. You do not publish a port for it. To use a different URL, set homegap.traefik_api.

Until the API answers for the first time, HomeGAP does not change the services. The error is the Traefik API at ... has not answered; set homegap.traefik_api if it is elsewhere. After the first answer, a failed read keeps the routers from the last good read.

items.title: Refused names
items.text:
HomeGAP refuses a name that covers the client address pangolin.<domain> or the management host of a node, with an error. A Pangolin client tries to reach its own server through the tunnel for such a name. Then it loses the connection on its next reconnect.

Thus HomeGAP refuses *.example.net. A sub-zone such as *.home is correct.

items.title: Example
items.text:
This compose example has the front door, the tunnels service and the private network:

services:
  traefik:
    labels:
      homegap.expose: "example.net"
      homegap.wildcard: "true"
      homegap.protocol: "https"
      homegap.proxy_protocol: "true"
      homegap.private_network: "homegap-private"
      homegap.private_middleware: "private-only@file"
      homegap.private_hosts: "*.home"
    networks: [traefik, homegap-private]
  tunnels:
    networks:
      traefik: { ipv4_address: 172.32.0.250 }
      homegap-private: {}

networks:
  homegap-private:
    ipam: { config: [ { subnet: 172.33.0.0/24 } ] }

The homegap.private_hosts label is optional.

items.title: Configure client addresses and private-only services
items.text:
1. Create the homegap-private network.
  2. Attach tunnels and the homelab Traefik to this network.
  3. Give tunnels a fixed address on the traefik network.
  4. Add proxyProtocol.trustedIPs to the entrypoint of Traefik.
  5. If you have terminated services, add forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs with the same address.
  6. Restart Traefik. These settings are in the static config.
  7. Add the labels to the front door.
  8. Add the allowlist middleware to the private-only routers.
  9. Set homegap.roles to the roles that get the private path.
  10. Do the checks in the next section.

items.title: Check the result
items.text:
From the public internet, do these checks:

  • A private-only name returns 403.
  • A public service shows your real IP address in X-Real-Ip. A whoami service can show this header.

From a device with the Pangolin client, do these checks:

  • The private-only name works.
  • The service sees an address in the private subnet.

items.title: On the VPN, a private-only name still returns 403
items.text:
The name has no private path. On the Config page, look at the desired state for hg-private-- resources. Also look at the log.

Make sure that the router uses the middleware by its name, on the router itself. HomeGAP reads the middleware list of the router. Or list the name in homegap.private_hosts.

items.title: Public traffic comes from the private subnet
items.text: The target of the front door is its private address. Set homegap.host, or keep the front door on only one other network.

items.title: Label reference
items.text: This page lists every homegap.* label, with its values, its default and its rules. It also tells you how to declare several services on one container.

items.title: Values
items.text:
Label values are text. For a boolean label, use true, 1, yes or on, or false, 0, no or off. The case is not important. Any other value gives the error <key> must be true/false.

For a label with a fixed set of values, any other value gives the error <key> must be one of ... (got '<value>').

items.title: Core labels
items.text: Label Values Default What it does homegap.expose A hostname. None. Each service needs it. Sets the hostname to expose, for example app.example.net, or the root example.net. HomeGAP changes it to lowercase. homegap.wildcard Boolean. false On the root entry, also claims *.<domain>. homegap.protocol http, https, tcp, udp, tcp+udp http, or raw if the port list has protocols. Sets the protocol of the service. For a raw service, it is the default protocol of the ports. homegap.port A port from 1 to 65535. For raw services, a port list. 443 for https, 80 for http. Sets the port of the container. Raw services need it. See Port lists. homegap.tls passthrough, terminate passthrough With passthrough, the node sees only the SNI. With terminate, the node ends TLS, and Pangolin sign-in is possible. homegap.regions Node ids, separated by commas. all Limits the service to these nodes, for example na1,as1. The value all or an empty value selects every node. homegap.access public, private public With private, only the Pangolin client can reach the service. homegap.auth none, sso, pin none Puts Pangolin sign-in in front of the service. homegap.maintenance_page Boolean. true with terminate. While the homelab is unreachable, the nodes show a "back shortly" page for the service. See Traffic paths. homegap.healthcheck An HTTP path that starts with /, or tcp. None. Sets the health check of the Pangolin target. On the front door, it also sets the path of the health resource that Bunny probes.

items.title: Rules for the core labels
items.text:
• homegap.expose must be a valid hostname. It must be inside domain, or you get the error "... is outside the managed domain ...".
  • homegap.wildcard is valid only when homegap.expose is the root domain. It is an error on raw services.
  • The node always terminates plain http. If you set homegap.tls: passthrough on an http service, you get the warning plain-http services cannot be passed through; the node terminates TLS (tls=terminate).
  • On raw services, homegap.tls has no effect. HomeGAP gives a warning.
  • An unknown node id in homegap.regions gives the warning "regions reference unknown node(s): ...".
  • homegap.auth needs homegap.tls: terminate. Without it, you get the error "...requires homegap.tls=terminate (the node cannot authenticate encrypted traffic)".
  • homegap.auth: pin needs homegap.pin_env.
  • homegap.maintenance_page needs homegap.tls: terminate. A passthrough service has no page, because the node holds no certificate for its name. If you set the label to true on a passthrough service, you get the error "...needs homegap.tls=terminate...".
  • If the front door has homegap.tls: terminate and homegap.wildcard, HomeGAP refuses homegap.tls: passthrough on another hostname one label under the domain. See Certificates.
  • Without homegap.healthcheck, Bunny still probes / through the front door. On raw services, the label applies only to the TCP ports.

items.title: Extension labels
items.text: Label Default What it does homegap.host The container name. Sets the host that the tunnel connects to. The container name must resolve on a network that the container shares with tunnels. homegap.public_port The value of homegap.port. Sets the public port on the nodes, for a raw service with a single port. homegap.roles None. Lists the Pangolin roles, separated by commas, that can use auth=sso, a private resource or a private path. homegap.pin_env None. Names an environment variable on the orchestrator that holds the 6-digit PIN for auth=pin. homegap.pause false With true, HomeGAP keeps the Pangolin resources and DNS records of this service as they are. It observes them, but it never changes them. homegap.proxy_protocol false Sends the address of each viewer to the service with PROXY protocol v2. homegap.private_network None. Names a Docker network that only tunnels and this service share. Pangolin clients reach the service at its address on that network. homegap.private_hosts The hostname of the service, if homegap.private_middleware is not set. Lists the names, separated by commas, that Pangolin clients reach through the private network. homegap.private_middleware None. Gives a private path to each name that this Traefik routes through this middleware, for example private-only@file. homegap.traefik_api http://<container name>:8080 Sets the URL of the API of this Traefik, for homegap.private_middleware. The form is http://<host>:<port>, with no path. The host must be a container name or a private IPv4 address. For other values, HomeGAP gives a warning and uses the default.

items.title: Rules for the extension labels
items.text:
• homegap.public_port on an http or https service gives the warning "... only applies to tcp/udp".
  • A hostname that HomeGAP routes itself is an error. These are the management host of a node, the client address of the cluster, and the names of the status page and the speed test. The error is hostname N is reserved for HomeGAP.
  • With more than one port, homegap.public_port is an error. Write public:port in homegap.port instead.
  • The node uses these ports itself: 22, 80, 443, 2379, 2380, 3000, 3001, 3002, 3003, 3004, 3005, 5432, 5433, 6379, 6380, 8008, 8080, 8082, 8090, 21820, 26379 and 51820. A public raw service cannot use them as public ports. The error is public port N is reserved on nodes; publish it on another port (public:port in homegap.port, or homegap.public_port). In cluster mode, cluster.mesh.port/udp is reserved too. HomeGAP does not check private services, because they publish nothing on the nodes.
  • HomeGAP removes Admin from the roles that it sends to Pangolin, because Pangolin refuses it there. The Admin role can reach everything.
  • The PIN must be a number from 100000 to 999999. If there is no PIN, or the PIN is not valid, HomeGAP writes an error to the log.
  • homegap.proxy_protocol works only on https services in passthrough mode and on raw services with TCP ports, and only on public services. On a raw service, it applies only to the TCP ports. See Client addresses and private-only services.
  • homegap.private_network works only on public http and https services.
  • homegap.private_hosts and homegap.private_middleware need homegap.private_network.
  • A name in homegap.private_hosts can be relative to the hostname of the service (jellyfin, *.home) or a full name. You can use * and ?.
  • homegap.private_middleware compares the middleware without its @provider part. HomeGAP reads the routers from the Traefik API.

items.title: Port lists
items.text:
For a raw service, homegap.port takes a list of entries, separated by commas. Each entry has this form:

[public:]port[/tcp|/udp|/tcp+udp]
Entry Meaning 7881 Port 7881, with the protocol from homegap.protocol. 7881/tcp Port 7881 on TCP. 3478/tcp+udp Port 3478 on TCP and on UDP. HomeGAP also reads udp+tcp as tcp+udp. 2222:22/tcp Public port 2222 on the nodes, to port 22 of the container, on TCP.

These rules apply:

  • A list with a protocol on an entry is a raw service, also without homegap.protocol. For example, homegap.port: "7881/tcp, 7882/udp" is enough.
  • homegap.protocol gives the protocol of the entries without their own protocol. With tcp+udp, each such port is on TCP and UDP. The protocol of an entry has priority.
  • Without homegap.protocol, each entry needs a protocol if one entry has one. Otherwise, you get the error '<entry>' needs a protocol (/tcp, /udp or /tcp+udp), or set homegap.protocol.
  • An http or https service takes only one port number. A list gives the error must be one port number for http services.
  • An entry that is not a port from 1 to 65535 gives an error with examples of valid entries.
  • The same public port and protocol twice in one service gives the error is listed twice.

The protocol of the service is the sum of its ports: tcp, udp or tcp+udp. The Services page shows the port list in the protocol column, for example 7881/tcp, 7882/udp. See Raw TCP and UDP.

items.title: Named services
items.text:
One container can declare several services. Put the labels of each service under homegap.services.<name>., for example homegap.services.alt.expose and homegap.services.alt.port. Every label works under this prefix, for example tls, access, auth, healthcheck, proxy_protocol and private_network.

These rules apply:

  • The name has lowercase letters, digits and dashes. It starts and ends with a letter or a digit, and it has 31 characters or fewer (^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,29}[a-z0-9])?$).
  • Each named service needs its own expose. Without it, you get the error services.<name>: homegap.expose is required.
  • The top-level labels of the container are still a service of their own, when homegap.expose is set.
  • A named service takes these top-level labels as its defaults: homegap.host, homegap.regions, homegap.access, homegap.roles and homegap.pause. It can set its own values.
  • The errors and warnings of a named service start with services.<name>:. An error drops only that service. The other services of the container still publish.
  • An unknown label under a named service gives a warning with the full name of the label.
  • The key of a named service is <host slug>--<name>. HomeGAP uses this key for pause, on the dashboard and in the DNS purpose. The Services page shows the container as <container> · <name>.

items.title: Shared hostnames and ports
items.text:
When two services claim the same thing, the first container in the order of names wins. HomeGAP refuses the later one with an error:

  • Only one http or https service can use a hostname.
  • Raw services can share a hostname with each other, and with one http or https service. DNS has one record set for the hostname, on every node that serves any of these services.
  • Two top-level services on one hostname have the same key. HomeGAP refuses the second one with the error ...already claimed by <container>; give this service a name under homegap.services.. Give the second service a name.
  • On the nodes that two public services share (by homegap.regions), only one service can use a public port and protocol. The error is public port 7882/udp is already used by <container> (<name>). On different nodes, the same port is valid.
  • A raw service on the root domain is never the front door.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The front door claims the root and the wildcard, with end-to-end TLS:

traefik:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "example.net"
    homegap.wildcard: "true"
    homegap.protocol: "https"
    homegap.tls: "passthrough"

A private raw TCP service for SSH, on its own subdomain, on two nodes:

ssh-jump:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "ssh.example.net"
    homegap.port: "22"
    homegap.protocol: "tcp"
    homegap.access: "private"
    homegap.regions: "na1,as1"

A public game server on UDP port 27015, in one region:

game:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "game.example.net"
    homegap.protocol: "udp"
    homegap.port: "27015"
    homegap.regions: "eu1"

A voice server with a port list, and a named service on the same hostname with a different public port:

rtc:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "rtc.example.net"
    homegap.port: "7881/tcp, 7882/udp, 3478/tcp+udp"
    homegap.services.alt.expose: "rtc.example.net"
    homegap.services.alt.port: "17000:7000/udp"

items.title: Private services
items.text: A private service is available only through the Pangolin client. This page tells you how HomeGAP publishes a private service in each mode.

items.title: How a private service works
items.text:
With homegap.access: private, the service becomes a Pangolin private resource in host mode. HomeGAP sets the resource like this:

  • The alias is the value of homegap.expose.
  • The destination is the value of homegap.host. The default is the container name.
  • The ports are the container ports from homegap.port, by protocol, as tcp-ports and udp-ports. For a raw service with a port list, a public: part has no effect here.

A private service has no public DNS record and no public port.

homegap.roles lists the Pangolin roles that can reach the service. The Admin role can always reach it.

A private service is different from the private path of a public service. A private service has no public path. For the private path, see Client addresses and private-only services.

items.title: Users and connections in each mode
items.text:
StandaloneCluster

Each node that serves the service has its own private resource, in its own Pangolin. The Pangolin app connects to the Pangolin of one node, at its management host https://pangolin-<id>.<domain>.

Users and roles are different on each node. You manage them in the Pangolin web UI of each node. To open that UI, use SSH port forwarding. See Manage nodes.

The Access page on the dashboard is for cluster mode only.

One private resource lists the site of every node that serves the service. The Pangolin app connects to pangolin.<domain>, and DNS sends it to the nearest healthy node. The app then relays through that node to the homelab.

The app selects the node when it connects or when it changes network. You manage the users on the Access page. See Users and devices.

items.title: Publish the dashboard as a private service
items.text:
Warning

If you publish the dashboard as a public service, everybody on the internet can reach the control of every node. Publish it only as a private resource.

Put the labels on the orchestrator service. It is on the traefik network. For example:

orchestrator:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "homegap.example.net"
    homegap.access: "private"
    homegap.protocol: "http"
    homegap.port: "8088"
    homegap.host: "orchestrator"

The destination of the private resource is orchestrator, the name of the service on the traefik network. The port is 8088.

The dashboard must listen on an address that the tunnels container can reach. The example config uses dashboard.bind: 0.0.0.0:8088. The default 127.0.0.1:8088 is not reachable from other containers.

From a device with the Pangolin client, open http://homegap.example.net:8088.

items.title: Reach the homelab host over SSH
items.text:
A private service can point at the homelab host itself, for example at its SSH server. Then the host accepts SSH from Pangolin clients, and the internet has no path to it.

The tunnels container opens the connection to the destination. Thus the host needs a name that the container can resolve. With host-gateway, Docker gives the name host.docker.internal the address of the host. This name stays correct when the LAN address of the host changes.

  1. In the compose file of the homelab, add extra_hosts and the labels to the tunnels service:

    tunnels:
  extra_hosts:
    - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "ssh.example.net"
    homegap.access: "private"
    homegap.protocol: "tcp"
    homegap.port: "22"
    homegap.host: "host.docker.internal"

  2. Start the container again. The connectors reconnect in a few seconds.

    docker compose up -d tunnels

  3. Check that the container can reach the SSH server of the host. The command prints open.

    docker compose exec tunnels bash -c 'timeout 3 bash -c "</dev/tcp/host.docker.internal/22" && echo open'

  4. On a device, connect the Pangolin app.

  5. Connect to the alias:

    ssh user@ssh.example.net

Port 22 is reserved on the nodes, but a private service has no public port, so HomeGAP accepts it. Without homegap.roles, only the Admin role can reach the host. To give access to other users, add their role, for example homegap.roles: "Member".

If the check in step 3 does not print open, look at the host:

  • sshd must listen on an address that the container can reach. The default ListenAddress (all addresses) is correct.
  • The firewall of the host must accept port 22 from the Docker networks. With ufw, run sudo ufw allow from 172.16.0.0/12 to any port 22 proto tcp.

Instead of host.docker.internal, homegap.host can be the LAN address of the host. Then extra_hosts is not necessary.

Warning

If the front door has a wildcard (homegap.wildcard), public DNS also answers for the alias, with the addresses of the nodes. A device that does not resolve the alias through the Pangolin app connects to the SSH server of a node. That server then receives your user name and your password or key. Before you accept a host key, compare its fingerprint with the key of the homelab host.

To read the fingerprint of the host key, run this command on the homelab host:

ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

items.title: Raw TCP and UDP
items.text: HomeGAP can publish a service that does not use HTTP, for example a game server, a voice server or an SSH jump host. This page tells you how raw TCP and UDP services work.

items.title: The labels
items.text:
A raw service needs these labels:

  • homegap.expose, with a hostname for the service.
  • homegap.port, the port or the list of ports of the container. Raw services need this label.
  • The protocol: homegap.protocol (tcp, udp or tcp+udp), or a protocol on each entry of the port list.

For example, these labels publish TCP 7881 and UDP 7882 without homegap.protocol:

homegap.expose: "voice.example.net"
homegap.port: "7881/tcp, 7882/udp"

For the format of the port list and its rules, see Port lists.

homegap.wildcard is an error on a raw service. homegap.tls has no effect. To limit the nodes that serve the service, use homegap.regions.

items.title: What HomeGAP creates
items.text:
For each port and protocol of a public raw service, HomeGAP creates these items on each node of the service:

  • A Pangolin resource.
  • A Traefik entrypoint.
  • A published Gerbil port.
  • A ufw rule.

The hostname also gets a geo DNS record set. Raw services that share a hostname share one record set. See Shared hostnames and ports.

items.title: Public ports
items.text:
The public port of an entry is its public: part. Without it, the public port is the same as the container port. For a service with a single port, homegap.public_port also sets the public port.

HomeGAP refuses public ports that the node uses itself. For the list, see the Label reference.

items.title: Resource ids
items.text:
Service niceId A top-level service with one port and one protocol hg-<host>-<proto>, for example hg-game-example-net-udp. Any other top-level service hg-<host>-<public port>-<proto>, for example hg-voice-example-net-7882-udp. A named service hg-<host>--<name>-<public port>-<proto>, for example hg-rtc-example-net--alt-17000-udp.

The first form is the id from before port lists. Thus an upgrade does not recreate the resources of existing services.

items.title: Health checks and client addresses
items.text:
homegap.healthcheck: tcp applies only to the TCP ports. UDP ports have no health check of their target.

homegap.proxy_protocol: "true" applies only to the TCP ports. The service must accept PROXY protocol v2. See Client addresses and private-only services.

A UDP service sees the address of the tunnels container, because there is no PROXY protocol for UDP. Each caller keeps its own path through the tunnel. In the end-to-end tests, two UDP callers at the same time each get their own reply, from different source ports. UDP payloads up to 1400 bytes pass in both directions, with tunnels.mtu: 1420.

Caution

A new raw port changes the stack of the node: a new entrypoint and a new Gerbil port. Thus HomeGAP updates the nodes one at a time. See Node updates and rollback.

items.title: Private raw services
items.text: With homegap.access: private, a raw service gets no public port and no DNS record. Only Pangolin clients can reach it. The private resource lists the container ports by protocol, as tcp-ports and udp-ports. A public: part has no effect there. See Private services.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
A public game server on UDP port 27015, only on eu1:

game:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "game.example.net"
    homegap.protocol: "udp"
    homegap.port: "27015"
    homegap.regions: "eu1"

A private SSH jump host on TCP port 22. Port 22 is reserved on the nodes, but a private service has no public port, so HomeGAP accepts it:

ssh-jump:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "ssh.example.net"
    homegap.port: "22"
    homegap.protocol: "tcp"
    homegap.access: "private"
    homegap.regions: "na1,as1"

A public SSH server on public port 2222, to port 22 of the container:

git-ssh:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "git.example.net"
    homegap.port: "2222:22/tcp"

A voice server with several ports, and a named service on the same hostname:

rtc:
  labels:
    homegap.expose: "rtc.example.net"
    homegap.port: "7881/tcp, 7882/udp, 3478/tcp+udp"
    homegap.services.alt.expose: "rtc.example.net"
    homegap.services.alt.port: "17000:7000/udp"

For a full example with a chat app and its voice server, see Fluxer.

items.title: Traffic paths
items.text: HomeGAP sends traffic to a service on one of several paths. This page tells you how each path works and when to use it.

items.title: Front door, passthrough
items.text:
This is the default path. The homelab Traefik claims the root domain and *.<domain>.

  1. On each node, a Traefik TCP router on :443 reads the TLS SNI. It matches the root and any single label under the domain.
  2. The router forwards the encrypted stream into the Pangolin TCP resource hg-frontdoor.
  3. The stream goes through the tunnel to the homelab Traefik.

The node holds no certificate for these names, so it cannot read the traffic. Your certificates stay at home.

The node serves some names itself, so the wildcard passthrough does not include them:

  • The management host of each node, pangolin-<id>.<domain>.
  • In cluster mode, the client address pangolin.<domain>.
  • The shared names of the status page and the speed test, status.<domain> and speedtest.<domain>. The node sends their requests on to the homelab under its own names, status-<node>.<domain> and speedtest-<node>.<domain>.
  • Dedicated hostnames that use terminate.

On port 80, the node sends a permanent redirect to HTTPS for the passthrough names.

Each passthrough resource has an internal proxy port on the node. The ports start at pangolin.passthrough_port_base (default 40000). HomeGAP never publishes these ports.

items.title: Front door, terminate
items.text:
